3.54.0 2026-07-31 22:45:45 bf44a08adc94b8c7c69921a1292d56bec0cbd9f3ac772e31d8ea5866e9f46063 (64-bit)

I see in pager.c that if the immutable flag is set, then the read-only flags are set, but that happens after the file has already been opened. Could this be done before, or could the documentation say something like "treats immutable databases as read-only"?

title: Bug in test suite

posts.author: drh
posts.body: check-in 273e1bcc2c669bc9.

posts.author: Dan Shearer (danshearer)
posts.body:
I thought I had a free-of-unallocated bug, but instead I think it is a test bug.

musl is a widely-used embedded libc. Alpine Linux uses it, and unlike glibc or FreeBSD libc it often doesn't leave memory lying around in the same place after a free. I observed this reproducer on Alpine Linux edge, x86-64, as an unprivileged user:
$ wget https://sqlite.org/2026/sqlite-src-3530400.zip
$ unzip -q sqlite-src-3530400.zip && cd sqlite-src-3530400
$ ./configure && make testfixture
$ valgrind ./testfixture test/capi3c.test 2>&1 | grep -A3 'Invalid read'

test/capi3c.test closes a database handle and then closes the same handle again, expecting SQLITE_MISUSE. Another 2 similar tests immediately following also fail if you run them manually. On Alpine they cause a segfault. This does not necessarily happen every time, but with musl most of the time as far as I have seen.

sqlite3.h says:

The C parameter to sqlite3_close(C) ... must be either a NULL pointer or an sqlite3 object pointer obtained from sqlite3_open() ... and not previously closed.

Therefore SQLITE_MISUSE can't be reliably returned, because an operating system can legitimately crash or otherwise error before SQLite gets to return anything. Just as it happens, the most common non-embedded platforms do not do so.

Building SQLite with -fsanitize=address on glibc and calling sqlite3_close() twice reports the same heap-use-after-free in sqlite3SafetyCheckSickOrOk, which is the same behaviour. I don't see a way of catching this without writing reference counting machinery, so I think its documented behaviour and the test is never going to be reliable.

Therefore I propose removing capi3c-3.6.1/2/3-misuse .

--
Dan Shearer
dan@shearer.org / https://shearer.org

title: FIX: Name collision in variables for building Tcl extension

posts.author: Dan Shearer (danshearer)
posts.body:
Variables set in tclConfig.sh come from Tcl's own config. Variables of exactly the same names are used in buildtclext.tcl but sometimes for different purposes. The colliding variables include: CC, CFLAGS, LDFLAGS, and SHLIB_CFLAGS.

When building SQLite's Tcl extension, if you're lucky and the your OS's template uses the same meaning for two of these variables and defines the others regardless of value, then it will work. On NetBSD and OpenBSD, and other OSs if they change their mind in the future, this is not the case and the extension won't build and so the test suite can't run.

Example:
$ gmake tclextension
can't read "SHLIB_CFLAGS": no such variable
while executing
"subst $cmd"
(file "tool/buildtclext.tcl" line 88)

The fix moves the variables sideways into EXTRA, and makes sure the variables are always defined no matter what a particular template does.
--- a/tool/buildtclext.tcl
+++ b/tool/buildtclext.tcl
@@ -167,9 +167,18 @@
}
set cmd {${CC} ${CFLAGS} ${LDFLAGS} -shared}
regexp {TCL_SHLIB_LD='([^']+)(-Wl,--out-implib.*)?'} $tclConfig all cmd
-  set LDFLAGS "$INC -DUSE_TCL_STUBS"
+
+  # TCL_SHLIB_LD is a shell command recorded from the Tcl build, so the names
+  # in it are Tcl's configure-time variables. We use every name that
+  # a tclConfig.sh is known to use so [subst] below doesn't fail.
+  set SHLIB_CFLAGS $CFLAGS
+  set LDFLAGS ""
+
+  # Our own options get appended to the command directly.
+
+  set EXTRA "$INC -DUSE_TCL_STUBS"
if {[string length $OPTS]>1} {
-    append LDFLAGS $OPTS
+    append EXTRA $OPTS
}
if {$tcl_platform(os) eq "Windows NT"} {
set OUT cyg
@@ -184,7 +193,11 @@
set @ $OUT; # Workaround for https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/0683a49cb02f31a1
# in which Gentoo edits their tclConfig.sh to include an soname
# linker flag which includes ${@} (the target file's name).
-  set CMD [subst $cmd]
+  if {[catch {subst $cmd} CMD]} {
+    puts stderr "warning: cannot expand TCL_SHLIB_LD: $CMD"
+    set CMD "$CC $CFLAGS -shared"
+  }
+  append CMD " $EXTRA"
}

# Check the SQLite TCL extension that is loaded by default by this running

--
Dan Shearer
dan@shearer.org / https://shearer.org

title: FIX: Autosetup find_tclconfig.tcl can't find tclConfig.sh

posts.author: Dan Shearer (danshearer)
posts.body:
On OpenBSD 7.9, ./configure cannot find tclConfig.sh although it is present and readable, so the test suite cannot be built. Using SQLite 3.53.4:
$ ./configure
Checking for tclsh8.6.../usr/local/bin/tclsh8.6
WARNING: /usr/local/bin/tclsh8.6 is unable to recommend a tclConfig.sh
WARNING: Found tclsh but no tclConfig.sh.

$ ls /usr/local/lib/tcl/tcl8.6/tclConfig.sh
/usr/local/lib/tcl/tcl8.6/tclConfig.sh

$ tclsh8.6 autosetup/find_tclconfig.tcl
cannot find tclConfig.sh in either /usr/local/lib or /usr/local/lib/tcl8.6

Here is a patch for autosetup, no OS-specific knowledge because there may be other OSs out there that store Tcl libs in unusual places... the patch uses the running Tcl's library tree as a starting point if existing paths fail.
--- a/autosetup/find_tclconfig.tcl
+++ b/autosetup/find_tclconfig.tcl
@@ -12,13 +12,15 @@
puts stderr "tclsh reported library directory \"$libdir\" does not exist"
exit 1
}
-if {![file exists $libdir/tclConfig.sh]} {
-  set n1 $libdir/tcl$::tcl_version
-  if {[file exists $n1/tclConfig.sh]} {
-    set libdir $n1
-  } else {
-    puts stderr "cannot find tclConfig.sh in either $libdir or $n1"
-    exit 1
+set candidates [list $libdir $libdir/tcl$::tcl_version]
+foreach d $::tcl_pkgPath {
+  lappend candidates $d $d/tcl$::tcl_version
+}
+foreach d $candidates {
+  if {[file exists $d/tclConfig.sh]} {
+    puts $d
+    exit 0
}
}
-puts $libdir
+puts stderr "cannot find tclConfig.sh in any of: [join $candidates {, }]"
+exit 1

--
Dan Shearer
dan@shearer.org / https://shearer.org

title: Uninitialized page-buffer disclosure via WAL/DB page-size mismatch (3.53.4)

posts.author: Winter (winter.cb)
posts.body:
A write-ahead log whose header declares a page size smaller than the
database's page size is accepted during WAL recovery without any
cross-check. On the read path the frame is short-read into a full-size
pager page buffer with no zero-fill of the tail, so the remainder of the
buffer retains whatever was previously in that page-cache slot. A record
on the affected page that declares a payload longer than the bytes
actually supplied by the frame then surfaces that recycled memory through
ordinary SQL (for example substr()), disclosing page-cache content that
was never part of the queried row.

Verified against the 3.53.4 release (the latest release at the time of
testing) on x86-64 Linux. The relevant wal.c code path was byte-identical
to trunk as of my audit on 16 August 2026, so this does not appear to be
fixed.

Because page-cache slots are recycled heap buffers, the disclosed bytes
are not limited to row data -- any prior page-cache content can be
exposed, including internal pointer material.

ROOT CAUSE

Two independent gaps combine:

In walIndexRecover() the WAL header page size is validated only as a
power of two in 512, SQLITE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE.
It is never compared against the page size declared in the database
header.
On the read path, readDbPage() passes the full database page size as
nOut into a full-size page buffer (src/pager.c:3082), but
sqlite3WalReadFrame() reads only the WAL's page size (src/wal.c:3672):

/* pager.c:3082, readDbPage() */
rc = sqlite3WalReadFrame(pPager->pWal, iFrame, pPager->pageSize,
pPg->pData);

/* wal.c:3672, sqlite3WalReadFrame() */
return sqlite3OsRead(pWal->pWalFd, pOut, (nOut>sz ? sz : nOut),
iOffset);

When the WAL page size (say 512) is smaller than the database page
size (say 4096), only 512 bytes are written and the remaining 3584
bytes of the buffer are never initialized on this path. There is no
memset of the unread tail, and page-cache buffers are recycled without
zeroing, so the tail holds prior cache content.

REPRODUCTION

Environment: SQLite 3.53.4, x86-64 Linux, default VFS, page cache
populated by prior queries (the normal state of any long-running
process).

Construct:

A database with page size 4096 in WAL mode, containing a table t(b).
A crafted -wal whose header declares page size 512 (valid magic,
salts, and checksums), with one commit frame for t's leaf page. The
512-byte frame holds a valid table-leaf header and a single record
whose one column is a BLOB declaring length 3000. Only ~486 bytes of
that BLOB body fit in the 512-byte frame; the rest is read from the
uninitialized page-buffer tail.

To make the disclosure observable and unambiguous, prime the page cache
with a recognisable marker before reading (a stand-in for other data a
real process would already have cached), then read the over-declared
blob:

PRAGMA cache_size=12;                     -- force buffer recycling

-- 'primer' holds rows full of the ASCII marker CANARY_LEAK_42_

SELECT count(*) FROM primer;              -- populate/recycle buffers

SELECT length(b) FROM t;                  -- 3000 (only ~486 from WAL)

SELECT hex(substr(b,520,120)) FROM t;     -- tail = recycled content

Observed result (tail decoded to ASCII):

...RY_LEAK_42_CANARY_LEAK_42_CANARY_LEAK_42_CANARY_LEAK_42_CANARY_LE...

The CANARY_LEAK_42_ marker belongs to table primer. It appears inside a
value read from table t. Content from one table has leaked into another
table's query result through the uninitialized page-buffer tail.

IMPACT NOTE

Weaponization is possible: when combined with a second, independent
defect in FTS5 (a heap overflow fixed on trunk as check-in 9cd4f9e920
but still present in the shipped 3.53.4 release), this disclosure
provides the address information needed to escalate to code execution
under ASLR/PIE. Details of the second defect and the combined chain have
been sent privately to drh@sqlite.org; I am holding them for coordinated
handling.

Body
Hello,

src/pcache.h opens a standard include guard but never actually defines the
guard macro, so the guard is non-functional:

#ifndef _PCACHE_H_
...
#endif /* _PCACHE_H_ */

There is no #define _PCACHE_H_ anywhere in the file — I checked the whole
file for _PCACHE_H_/#define and the macro is only ever referenced by the
opening #ifndef and the closing #endif comment, never defined. As
written, every #include "pcache.h" re-enters and re-processes the entire
body of the header, because the guard condition is always true.

Why this is currently harmless
In the amalgamation build (the way most consumers build SQLite) this header
is only textually included once, so the missing #define has no observable
effect today. I'm reporting it because the guard reads as protecting
against double-inclusion but doesn't, which could surprise anyone building
against the split (non-amalgamation) source tree who includes pcache.h
from more than one translation unit's shared header, or refactors code
under the assumption the guard actually works.

Suggested fix
Add the missing definition, mirroring every other header in the tree:

#ifndef _PCACHE_H_
#define _PCACHE_H_
...
#endif /* _PCACHE_H_ */

Disclosure
This was found during a static-analysis study of the SQLite source and the
analysis/triage was assisted by an AI tool; I have manually verified the
code against current trunk before reporting. Happy to provide any further
detail.

Thanks,
Brandon Arrendondo

the report.

CREATE TABLE t0(c0 INTEGER, c1 AS (c0 * 5));

SELECT (t0.c1 IN (VALUES (1), (0.5 IS true)))
OR (t0.c1 IN (WITH w AS (SELECT 1) SELECT * FROM w))

WHERE (t0.c1 IN (VALUES (1), (0.5 IS true)))

title: Geopoly accepts non-finite polygons and its RTree optimization misses rows

posts.author: XingWang xiang (v3rdant)
posts.body:
Summary
geopoly_regular() accepts positive infinity as its radius and derives NaN
coordinates. The shape passes Geopoly's structural validation and can be
inserted normally. Its NaN bounding box is stored in the underlying RTree.

A bare geopoly_overlap() predicate uses the RTree optimization and silently
prunes the row. The same scalar predicate in a forced full scan returns true
for that row. Indexed SELECT and DELETE therefore disagree with full-scan
execution on an intact database.

This is a Release-visible logical index-consistency bug. It does not require a
malformed BLOB, direct shadow-table writes, a corrupt database, or a custom
extension.

Affected version
Reproduced on SQLite 3.53.3 Debug, optimized Release, and ASan+UBSan builds,
and on the checked 2026-08-16 master revision. All runs exited normally and
PRAGMA integrity_check returned ok.

Reproduction
Use a SQLite shell built with SQLITE_ENABLE_GEOPOLY:
sqlite3 :memory: < reproduce.sql

Expected observations:

scalar geopoly_overlap() reports overlap for the non-finite row;
the optimized query plan returns only row 1 (finite-control);
adding unary + disables the Geopoly constraint and the full scan returns
rows 1 and 2;
PRAGMA integrity_check still reports ok.

reproduce.sql is sufficient for the report.
-- reproduce.sql
.bail on
.headers on
.mode quote

SELECT sqlite_version() AS version, sqlite_source_id() AS source_id;
SELECT compile_options
FROM pragma_compile_options
WHERE compile_options GLOB '*DEBUG*'
OR compile_options GLOB '*GEOPOLY*'
OR compile_options GLOB '*RTREE*'
ORDER BY 1;

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE g USING geopoly(label);
INSERT INTO g(rowid,_shape,label) VALUES
(1,geopoly_regular(0,0,1e38,4),'finite-control'),
(2,geopoly_regular(0,0,1e999,4),'nonfinite-trigger');

SELECT rowid, label, typeof(_shape) AS shape_type, length(_shape) AS shape_len,
hex(_shape) AS shape_hex, geopoly_json(_shape) AS rendered,
geopoly_overlap(_shape,geopoly_regular(0,0,1,4)) AS scalar_overlap
FROM g ORDER BY rowid;

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT rowid,label FROM g
WHERE geopoly_overlap(_shape,geopoly_regular(0,0,1,4));
SELECT 'optimized' AS path, coalesce(group_concat(rowid||':'||label,','),'EMPTY')
AS rows_seen
FROM g
WHERE geopoly_overlap(_shape,geopoly_regular(0,0,1,4));

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT rowid,label FROM g
WHERE +geopoly_overlap(_shape,geopoly_regular(0,0,1,4));
SELECT 'forced-fullscan' AS path,
coalesce(group_concat(rowid||':'||label,','),'EMPTY') AS rows_seen
FROM g
WHERE +geopoly_overlap(_shape,geopoly_regular(0,0,1,4));

PRAGMA integrity_check;

title: Lemon: no--D invocation triggers glibc qsort() nonnull diagnostic in a downstream UBSan build

posts.author: yqtian
posts.body:
I encountered this while building a real downstream project.

Lighttpd vendors a copy of Lemon and
runs it during the ordinary parser-generation target in its CMake build to
generate configparser.c from configparser.y. The checked-in command is:
lemon -q -d<build-dir> -T<src-dir>/lempar.c <src-dir>/configparser.y

It has no Lemon -D options.

The first failure was reproduced from Lighttpd check-in
2ddc51389a139d2b08daf310596c951c1d53dc8d on Ubuntu 24.04 (glibc 2.39),
using Clang 18.1.3 and the standard UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer group in a
strict, non-recovering configuration:
cmake -S . -B build-ubsan \
-DWITH_PCRE2=OFF \
-DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang \
-DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-O1 -g -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined"
cmake --build build-ubsan -j6

The build reaches the ordinary parser-generation step and then stops:
[ 48%] Generating configparser.c from configparser.y
src/lemon.c:1813:9: runtime error: null pointer passed as argument 1,
which is declared to never be null
/usr/include/stdlib.h:971:30: note: nonnull attribute specified here
SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior src/lemon.c:1813:9
gmake[2]: *** [build/CMakeFiles/lighttpd.dir/build.make:76:
build/configparser.c] Error 1

I then checked the current canonical Lemon source in SQLite. The same call is
present in SQLite check-in
d287358b8d356d4fd3643b6776c56c6a6fdfb175834351eaed0148db4079dc67
(2026-08-18 15:13:10 UTC), in tool/lemon.c.

With no Lemon -D options, the globals retain their initial values:
static int nDefine = 0;
static char **azDefine = 0;

Lemon then calls:
qsort(azDefine, nDefine, sizeof(azDefine[0]), defineCmp);

Thus the documented and downstream-used no--D invocation reaches
qsort(NULL, 0, ..., defineCmp). The installed glibc declaration marks the
first and fourth parameters of qsort() nonnull, and Clang's
nonnull-attribute sanitizer diagnoses the call.

A minimal way to avoid the call only when the array is null is:
-  qsort(azDefine, nDefine, sizeof(azDefine[0]), defineCmp);
+  if( nDefine>0 )
+    qsort(azDefine, nDefine, sizeof(azDefine[0]), defineCmp);

I validated this exact guard in the downstream build with:
- Clang 18 annotation sanitizers: baseline build exit 2; patched build exit 0
- the patched build produced the Lighttpd executable
- no annotation-sanitizer diagnostic remained
- generated configparser.h was byte-identical
- generated configparser.c was identical after normalizing source-path-only
metadata
- the current SQLite tree with this exact guard passed its non-root `devtest`:
977,544 tests, 0 errors, exit 0

I also compiled current SQLite Lemon independently with GCC 13 and Clang 18.
With -fsanitize=nonnull-attribute and no -D, the baseline exits at the
qsort() call and the guarded version succeeds. For each of the zero-, one-,
and two--D cases, the baseline and guarded versions generate identical
parser content under ordinary compiler settings.

For completeness, the standard -fsanitize=undefined Lighttpd build shown
above contains a second, independent Lemon diagnostic involving an
incompatible function-pointer call after this first issue is removed. The
proposed guard removes the qsort()/nonnull failure but is not claimed to make
every UBSan check in the vendored Lemon copy clean. When the annotation checks
are isolated, the baseline downstream build fails at this call and the guarded
build completes as described above.

title: scanstatus2.test 5.x crashes the testfixture on every Windows build: `ptr:%p` key vs `format "ptr:0x%llx"` lookup

posts.author: anonymous
posts.body:
Version: 3.54.0 (checkout 93f6407070820d08e6c326e85473a1198e047d68)
Affects: any Windows build of testfixture with SQLITE_ENABLE_STMT_SCANSTATUS and the trace capability. Confirmed by inspection to be compiler-independent; measured with three toolchains (below).
Impact: hard crash (access violation), not a test failure — the run aborts and every remaining test in the file is skipped.

Summary
test/scanstatus2.test tests 5.0–5.2 register a trace_v2 callback that reconstructs a statement handle as a string, then passes it back into sqlite3_stmt_scanstatus. The string it builds does not match the one the pointer registry stored, so the lookup misses, pStmt is NULL, and sqlite3_stmt_scanstatus_v2() dereferences it.

The two spellings agree only when the C library's %p happens to emit 0x-prefixed, minimal-width lowercase hex. glibc and macOS do; no Windows C runtime does.

The mismatch
src/test1.c:78 — the registry key:
sprintf(aKey, "ptr:%p", pPtr);

test/scanstatus2.test:267-268 — the lookup key:
proc trace {stmt sql} {
set ptr [format "ptr:0x%llx" $stmt]

testStringToPointer() (src/test1.c:92) looks zStr up in the Tcl_HashTable and returns 0 on a miss. getStmtPointer() propagates that 0 into pStmt and still returns TCL_OK, so the caller proceeds and calls sqlite3_stmt_scanstatus_v2(pStmt=NULL, ...), which dereferences a Vdbe* field.

Measured %p output (sprintf(b, "ptr:%p", &x))

toolchain
output

MSVC (cl, VS 2022/18, x64)
ptr:0000007BD12FFB50

mingw-w64 gcc, default (__USE_MINGW_ANSI_STDIO)
ptr:00007ffffe2ffedc

mingw-w64 gcc, -D__USE_MINGW_ANSI_STDIO=0
ptr:00007FFFFE2FFEDC

glibc (Linux, for contrast)
ptr:0x55f10ad6f3a8

None of the Windows forms carry 0x, and all are zero-padded to 16 digits. format "ptr:0x%llx" produces ptr:0x7ffffe2ffedc. The lookup therefore always misses on Windows.

Reproduction
On Linux the test passes, which is why this is easy to miss:
$ ./testfixture test/scanstatus2.test
...
0 errors out of 24 tests

On Windows (any compiler), scanstatus2-5.1 faults. Under Wine the report is explicit about the null dereference:
wine: Unhandled page fault on read access to 0000000000000088

Address 0x88 is the offset of the Vdbe field read from the null pStmt.

A minimal confirmation that isolates the cause to the string spelling alone, run against one unmodified testfixture binary:
sqlite3 db :memory:
db eval {CREATE TABLE t1(x); INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1);}
set stmt [sqlite3_prepare db "SELECT * FROM t1" -1 TAIL]
sqlite3_step $stmt
puts "registry spelling: $stmt"           ;# ptr:00007FFFFF925998

# A: the registry's own spelling — works
catch {sqlite3_stmt_scanstatus -flags complex $stmt 0} r
puts "A rc=0, no crash"

# B: the spelling scanstatus2.test builds for the same pointer — crashes
set num [expr {"0x[string range $stmt 4 end]"}]
sqlite3_stmt_scanstatus -flags complex [format "ptr:0x%llx" $num] 0

Arm A returns cleanly; arm B faults at the same address. Same binary, same pointer, two spellings.

Suggested fixes
Any one of these closes it; the first is the smallest and keeps the two sides honest by construction:

Have the test ask for the handle string instead of building one. The pointer→string direction already exists and is what the registry keys on; the Tcl side just needs to use it rather than re-deriving a format.
Make testPointerToString() build a portable key — e.g. sprintf(aKey, "ptr:0x%llx", (unsigned long long)(uintptr_t)pPtr) — so the key no longer depends on %p, which is implementation-defined.
Make testStringToPointer() accept both spellings (normalise case, optional 0x, leading zeros).

Independently of which is chosen, it may be worth having getStmtPointer() report a failed lookup rather than returning TCL_OK with a NULL pStmt. Today a registry miss turns into a null dereference three frames later; an error there would have made this a one-line test failure instead of a crash that takes the rest of the file with it. SQLITE_ENABLE_API_ARMOR also makes the callee null-safe, but the test builds do not define it.

Note
Found while running the unmodified upstream test suite against a third-party compiler. The crash is not compiler-specific — it reproduces with MSVC and mingw-w64 as well, and the %p table above is the reason. Only the test harness is affected; nothing in the library itself is implicated.

title: ext/misc/normalize.c: __GCC__ typo leaves deliberate_fall_through inactive

posts.author: yqtian
posts.body:
I found this issue, and I reproduced and validated it against SQLite check-in
47774fd90b0d97ce9d5211dee0194a9c3eea95be.

The fallthrough annotation in ext/misc/normalize.c is never enabled by GCC because its preprocessor guard checks __GCC__:
#if !defined(deliberate_fall_through) && defined(__GCC__) && __GCC__>=7
# define deliberate_fall_through __attribute__((fallthrough));
#else
# define deliberate_fall_through
#endif

GCC defines __GNUC__,
not __GCC__. This block was introduced by check-in 08b920866073679ca4c22b184240dee27404cb08 on 2020-08-10 with the message "Fix harmless compiler warnings that surface in newer versions of GCC." Consequently, the two deliberate_fall_through uses added by that check-in have not performed their intended job under GCC. The current guard also leaves them inactive under Clang.

The GCC failure can be reproduced from a configured SQLite checkout using the standalone CLI mode in normalize.c:
gcc -std=c11 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Werror \
-DSQLITE_NORMALIZE_CLI ext/misc/normalize.c -lsqlite3 \
-o sql-normalize

GCC reports both intended fallthroughs as errors:
ext/misc/normalize.c:441:9: error: this statement may fall through
ext/misc/normalize.c:528:9: error: this statement may fall through

I reproduced this with GCC 7.5.0, GCC 11.4.0, and GCC 16.2.0. GCC emits both warnings under ordinary -Wall -Wextra; adding the common -Werror policy turns them into a build failure.

Clang 14.0.0 also reports both sites when implicit-fallthrough checking is enabled explicitly:
clang -std=c11 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wimplicit-fallthrough -Werror \
-DSQLITE_NORMALIZE_CLI ext/misc/normalize.c -lsqlite3 \
-o sql-normalize

One possible repair is to reuse the feature-check pattern already present in src/sqliteInt.h and ext/fts3/fts3Int.h:
/* Disable nuisance warnings about case fall-through */
-#if !defined(deliberate_fall_through) && defined(__GCC__) && __GCC__>=7
-# define deliberate_fall_through __attribute__((fallthrough));
-#else
+#if !defined(deliberate_fall_through)
+# if defined(__has_attribute)
+#  if __has_attribute(fallthrough)
+#   define deliberate_fall_through __attribute__((fallthrough));
+#  endif
+# endif
+#endif
+#if !defined(deliberate_fall_through)
# define deliberate_fall_through
#endif

With this change, the strict standalone build succeeds under GCC 7.5, GCC 11.4, GCC 16.2, and Clang 14.0.

For a behavior-preservation check, I linked the original and changed standalone programs against the tested revision's own libsqlite3.a and ran both over this input:
SELECT x'0123', .5, NULL FROM t WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3);
SELECT "quoted", x FROM tab WHERE x IS NULL;
INSERT INTO t VALUES(1, 'private text', 2.5);

The normalized outputs were byte-identical (SHA-256 756b1f643b470daf94c2d1eb351a7dad05137ea54439a5949d9a4d212d016c42).

This appears to be a build-portability issue in the maintained optional normalize.c extension and its standalone CLI, not a runtime-correctness issue in the SQLite core. Would the existing __has_attribute(fallthrough) pattern be the preferred repair here?

(happened both debug and release.) Depending on the mode the cflags are merged.

SQLITE_DISABLE_FTS3_UNICODE SQLITE_DISABLE_FTS4_DEFERRED SQLITE_DISABLE_PAGECACHE_OVERFLOW_STATS
$(BUILDPATH)/sqlite3.c:
sqlite/configure --disable-shared --disable-static --disable-json --disable-math --disable-threadsafe --disable-carray --disable-readline && \
make sqlite3.c

$(BUILDPATH)/sqlite3.o: $(BUILDPATH)/sqlite3.c
$(CC) $(CFLAGS_BASE) $(CFLAGS_RELEASE) $(addprefix -D, $(SQLITE_DEFINES)) -o $@ -c $<

sqlite3_objects = $(BUILDPATH)/sqlite3.o
main: $(sqlite3_objects)
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(LDFLAGS) $^ -o '$@'

some simplification here, but the args and flags are correct.

in release mode the .o is LTO'd into the main executable, but it looks like my debug build doesn't do that - it's kept as a separate lib linked (statically) into the executable. Both have the SIGBUS issue. For --disable-threadsafe, I don't use threads.

The main app does do PRAGMA optimize occasionally, if that might conflict with the defines. Generally, the intent was to omit CLI things, and unneeded functions (JSON, math, ..) for file size reasons, because building into the executable.

Gentoo, running 6.18.38, gcc 15.1, glibc 2.43, binutils 2.46.x.

-std=c23

Just to rule this out as a suspect: please try without that flag. SQLite is historically C89 and, as of a year or so ago, C99.

SQLITE_OMIT_...

And without some of those OMIT flags, please. Those are very specifically unsupported.

If you can reproduce this with a conventional build, it's much more likely to gain traction. The recent flood of LLM-driven tickets in this forum is sucking away all team bandwidth for chasing down, e.g., obscure combinations of OMIT which may or may not work together.

title: NULL pointer dereference on a SQL NULL vocabulary entry in amatchNext() (ext/misc/amatch.c)

posts.author: Brandon Arrendondo (arrendbm)
posts.body:
Body
Hello,

I believe there is a NULL pointer dereference in amatchNext() in
ext/misc/amatch.c (the approximate_match virtual table's cursor
advance), present on current trunk, that is triggerable by ordinary SQL
data (a NULL value), not just by OOM.

The defect
if( zNextIn[0] && zNextIn[0]!='*' ){
...
rc = sqlite3_step(p->pVCheck);
if( rc==SQLITE_ROW ){
zW = (const char*)sqlite3_column_text(p->pVCheck, 0);
if( strncmp(zBuf, zW, nWord+nNextIn)==0 ){       /* site 1 */
...
}
}
...
}

while( 1 ){
...
rc = sqlite3_step(p->pVCheck);
if( rc!=SQLITE_ROW ) break;
zW = (const char*)sqlite3_column_text(p->pVCheck, 0);
...
if( strncmp(zW, zBuf, nWord)!=0 ) break;             /* site 2 */
...
}

p->pVCheck is a statement compiled earlier in the same function as
SELECT "<zVocabWord>" FROM "<zVocabTab>" WHERE "<zVocabWord>">=?1 ...,
where zVocabTab/zVocabWord are the backing vocabulary table/column
supplied when the approximate_match virtual table is created. If that
row's selected column value is SQL NULL, sqlite3_column_text() returns
NULL, and both sites pass it straight to strncmp() with no check.

Reachability
sqlite3_column_text() returns NULL either on OOM or, per its documented
contract, "if the result is NULL". Nothing in this function's query
(WHERE "word">=?1) excludes NULL — a NULL value in the vocabulary word
column sorts and compares under SQLite's normal NULL-ordering rules and can
be selected as a row here. No special encoding is needed to reach this: any
approximate_match virtual table built over a vocabulary table containing
a NULL word entry crashes on the first lookup that reaches that row.

Suggested fix
Guard both sites, e.g.:

zW = (const char*)sqlite3_column_text(p->pVCheck, 0);
if( zW && strncmp(zBuf, zW, nWord+nNextIn)==0 ){
...
}

and equivalently for the second site (treating a NULL zW as "no match",
consistent with how the rest of the loop treats a non-matching row).

Disclosure
This was found during a static-analysis study of the SQLite source and the
analysis/triage was assisted by an AI tool; I have manually verified the
code against current trunk before reporting. Happy to provide any further
detail.

Thanks,
Brandon Arrendondo
